utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. When we began this trial a year ago, Your Honours may recall the first witness who testified, and on the very last day of his testimony he was asked about the experience and he said -- he was our first witness from Prijedor -- he told us, "When I was talking on Friday, mentioning the names of my friends, with the mention of every name I would see in my mind the person, and after that I spent a sleepless night. It's so exhausting and so painful that only a person who has been through something like that himself can understand. If somebody asked me, would I go back there? I would say that it is the people who make up a town, and the people who lived there are missing. I can't walk through Prijedor without meeting Nedzad Seric who would take his hat off for me, Osman Mahmuljin, Mr. Sadikovic, Esad. You don't know what it takes me not to cry here, what it costs me." Your Honour, this trial is about -- I have in my hand here one of our exhibits, one of our documents, S282. This trial is about these people that are missing from Prijedor. We've heard the names of a minority of these people even mentioned in the trial. I could probably only remember myself now a handful of them, but the case is about every one of them. It's about the victims of a campaign that one can see from the magnitude of it was organised, it was premeditated, it had the objective of changing forever the demographics of Prijedor. And in just a few months, it had great, great success in doing that. This case is about the role of Dr. Stakic in that organised criminal campaign, a campaign that the evidence has showed involved coordination among many people and principally coordination between the military, the police, and the civilian government, the civilian authorities in Prijedor and above but in Prijedor headed by Dr. Stakic. The objective of this campaign was to forever change the composition of Prijedor. It rises to the level of genocide because the campaign was intended to destroy the Croat and particularly the Muslim communities that had become the majority of persons in Prijedor. In that campaign, Your Honours know that in addition to the thousands of people, many, most of which are mentioned by name in this book, thousands were killed or are missing. The campaign is manifested in the fact that the crimes were done to make sure that community did not exist any longer in Prijedor by destroying the homes, by destroying the places of worship of those people. It was manifested by destroying whole sections of the municipality that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were traditionally inhabited by those people of historical significance, places like Kozarac and Stari Grad, and by even hiding the bodies of those who were the victims, making sure that there were -- would be no reason to return, no homes to go back to, no houses of worship, not even the graves of the loved ones to visit. But this case is not about other things that many people have misunderstood. And I think it's important to mention that. First of all, this case is not a case against the Serbian people of Prijedor or the Serbian people of Bosnia. In fact, in the evidence that we've heard in this case, we've heard of real heroes, Serbs, who did not buy into the campaign, who helped their neighbours, in some cases saved their lives. If you recall Dr. Merdzanic was talking about the bombardment of Kozarac. He mentioned the Serb who was in the hospital at the clinic helping. Do you remember the story of Witness X, and his horrible suffering? He was found and saved by two Serb soldiers. They acted properly as soldiers. It's never been our case that every member of the Serbian army is a war criminal. By no means. There are people who acted nobly. There are even people who fought nobly and according to the rules of war. Nusret Sivac was asked by the Defence about one of their own witnesses what he thought of that person and how he could be friends with them. And he said although this person was a Serb a very proud Serb and believed in the Serbian cause, he said that he was a good man and Mr. Sivac said, one day he wants to write a book "Good people in the time of evil." And many, many of our witnesses have talked about the help they received sometimes in hiding or in fleeing Prijedor from people that they couldn't name because it's still, unfortunately, too dangerous to name some of the people who were against that campaign of genocide and who assisted their neighbours in humane ways. It also has never been our case that Dr. Stakic is alone responsible. A campaign of this magnitude is not carried out by a single individual. A genocidal campaign requires organisation, coordination, military and political cooperation, and no one person is going to be responsible. We do not see this as mitigating the guilt of the accused. In most legal systems, it's recognised that crimes committed jointly in an enterprise are the most dangerous. Many, many legal systems aggravate the punishment for a crime committed with others in a group because society recognises that a group acting together is a greater danger and, as in this case, much, much greater damage can be done. It's not our case that this joint criminal enterprise existed only in Prijedor, and clearly we presented some evidence of orders and instructions that were passed on to Prijedor, usually through Dr. Stakic, from higher political authorities and some military commands passed on from higher military authorities, but these were carried out by the individuals in Prijedor. And we have concentrated our case and our evidence on what happened in that locality. What our case has shown is the close cooperation in Prijedor between the civilian authorities headed by Dr. Stakic, the military, that being the 43rd Brigade, and the Kozara Light Brigade, generally headed by Colonel Arsic, Major, later Colonel Zeljaja, and the police who during our indictment were headed by Simo Drljaca. This case is not about borders, politics, the dissolution of Yugoslavia. That formed the background of this case. Undoubtedly it affected events, and many of the motivations for the crime, the motivation for the campaign, arose out of these political events. But we're not here to decide political questions. We're not here, the International Community, to decide in this Tribunal, this criminal tribunal, on borders, political structures, the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We're here because the Security Council recognised that horrible crimes were happening in Bosnia. In 1993 the Security Council passed Resolution 827 and talked about -- expressed its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread and flagrant violations of international humanitarian law, the systematic detention, mass killings, rape of women, and continuance of the practice of ethnic cleansing. It was recognised that there was a need to deter that conduct in order to have peace, and the council said, determined to put an end to such crimes and to bring to justice the persons most responsible with the aim of contributing to the restoration and maintenance of peace this Tribunal was created. We're here because -- not because of politics but because of crimes, not because of an individual's desire to live within one state or another but the means by which that was carried out in Prijedor was criminal. You can't change borders by expelling people from the homes they lived in for generations. You cannot change borders by killing, by raping, by detaining, by destroying the community that had lived side by side with you. We know that when the -- in the SDS convention - and I may have the date wrong, but I believe it was the 12th of May, the sixteenth convention of the SDS party or the Assembly of -- the Serb Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina - Dr. Karadzic listed the six strategic objectives, and the very first of those objectives was the separation of nationalities. And our case is about how that objective was carried out in Prijedor and the criminal way in which it was carried out. I'm sure Your Honours have asked and many have asked - I've asked myself - why was Prijedor probably the worst example of a campaign of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina? What is it about Prijedor? We've met in this trial about 90 people from Prijedor, and we know there's nothing barbaric, there's nothing uncivil about Prijedor. We know something about its history. We know that the people from all sides are sophisticated, that they have humanity. How could so much killing and so much cruelty take place in that town? Why was Prijedor targeted for such a brutal campaign? And I think the answer lies perhaps in the fact in -- partly in the fact that Prijedor was just the opposite, was such a place where people for so long had gotten along so well, that those who wanted to separate nationalities, those who needed to create hatred and division had a particular challenge in Prijedor, where there was a long tradition of co-existence, intermarriage, friendship between ethnic groups. Prijedor was famous throughout the former Yugoslavia for the events of World War II and for the Partisan resistance in Kozara, Mount Kozara. We know there is a famous movie about the resistance at Mount Kozara. And we know that when Ante Markovic launched his campaign for the Reform Party with the goal of preserving Yugoslavia, it wasn't by coincidence that he chose Prijedor to launch that campaign, because Prijedor was seen as, if not the birthplace, one of the models of brotherhood and unity of the co-existence of people from different ethnic groups living together. And for those with a radical Serb nationalist agenda, Prijedor posed a particular problem because within the Krajina region we know that in the 1990 elections it was only Prijedor that the Muslims or Bosniaks had controlled -- had won enough seats to control the assembly. It came as a great shock to the Serbs, who through all the censuses until that time, through the 1980 census, were the majority, that the Muslims won the majority of seats in Prijedor. And then in the 1991 census, it was revealed that the Muslims had now become a plurality, that they had about 44 per cent of the population of the municipality and Serbs were second with about a little over 42 per cent, 42 and a half, and Croats had slightly less than 6 per cent. And also in those 1990 elections, Prijedor distinguished itself from many other places in Bosnia, and particularly in the Krajina, in that the non-national parties had their best showing in Prijedor. They won a third of the seats, while on a national basis these left bloc or non-national parties had only won about 10 per cent of the seats. So to rid Prijedor of that community, it was also necessary to destroy not just a few individuals, not just the people that could defend or resist, but it also became necessary and particularly targeted were those people that represented this long tradition of co-existence, of getting along and of peaceful inter-ethnic relations. And in our case we've seen tragically, ironically, but I think very intentionally these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people who most promoted inter-ethnic relations from the Muslim side were targeted. Dr. Stakic played a key, a crucial role in these events, having the top political position. Dr. Stakic is not, as the Defence sometimes tried to portray him, an innocent, a naive young man at the time. I find it a bit ironic. He was a 29-year-old doctor. At the same time, Dr. Stakic is being portrayed as a naive young man. All evil of the SDA party is purported to be coordinated by Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, who also was 29 years old, a 29-year-old doctor. Dr. Stakic was not dragged into politics. He jumped into politics and his career shows great ambition. We know that he started his political career in his home area of Omarska Maricka by being the founder of the People's Radical Party of Nikola Pasic. At the time of the 1990 -- and he became the first president of that party. It became apparent by the time of the 1990 elections that the leading force for the Serb nationalists was going to be the SDS, and at that time it's clear that Dr. Stakic merged his party or himself individually but appears merged his party because we see no other evidence of that party existing afterwards, with the SDS and got himself on the ballot of the SDS party. At times I've found it rather incredible that the Defence has maintained that Dr. Stakic was not a member of the SDS. From the time of the 1990 elections until the time he was arrested, it's quite clear he was a member of the SDS. He appears on the ballot in 1990 for the SDS. Following the election and the division of posts, he was made the vice-president of the municipal assembly on behalf of the SDS. He was elected on the 11th of September, 1991 the vice-president of the SDS party. He received - and I believe the document for later reference is S94 - he received by far the greatest number of votes in that election and he was made the vice-president. We know that, as I'll come to later, that he represented the SDS with higher authorities, with republic-level authorities. He attended meetings of the main board of the SDS. In 1996, he came back to power, was named again president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor with the backing of Dr. Karadzic, again as a member of the SDS. Mr. Kuruzovic, himself an SDS member from the very beginning and to this day, expressed surprise at Mr. Lukic's question that Dr. Stakic had been in the radical party. He had forgotten all about it. Dr. Stakic, not just throughout the indictment period but since the 1990 elections, all the way -- the evidence which suggests until his arrest was a member of the SDS - and when I say the evidence suggests until his arrest, I'd ask to have the computer monitor be turned on and refer Your Honours to a couple of the items found with Dr. Stakic at the time of his arrest. This first -- it's two different documents. I'm referring to one on the top. It was a card, an SDS card that was found on him. This is Exhibit S235-12. There were other cards. If we could have the next exhibit. S235-21, we see three different cards, all showing on his person at the time of his arrest Dr. Stakic was -- well, at least there's an expression in American English, a card-carrying member, of the SDS party. In document S101, Dr. Stakic was elected to represent Prijedor to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly. S100 is a document that shows that Dr. Stakic reported to the Prijedor SDS regarding a meeting he attended of the republic-level main board. Document S94 shows Dr. Stakic being selected to attend an SDS republic-level convention. Ms. Sutherland tells me it's S93, but I'm sure Your Honours will find it, whichever one. Many people, many of the witnesses have described Dr. Stakic's personality. What we know about him is that he was not a person -- he was not loud. He was a person of measured words. He was intelligent. His career shows he was ambitious. All the evidence would suggest he was diligent in carrying out his duties. He kept himself informed. He attended meetings. We learned from his driver that he travelled throughout the municipality to Banja Luka. We know many individuals came to meet him in his office, such as Mr. Marjanovic, Mr. Travar used to go to see him. Everything that we know about Dr. Stakic suggests that he was aware, he was independent, he was functioning in real power in the positions that he held. And I want to talk briefly about those positions, but I'd like to briefly mention that we have talked a lot in this trial about the legal powers of these various positions, and we've looked at statutes of the municipality, we've looked at the decisions on the formation of the Crisis Staff. But I'd caution Your Honours to remember we're not dealing with the regime that respected the rule of law. We're talking about a time of conflict and a time when the worst violations of law were occurring, coordinated by the top authorities. The law was not respected. Law was used at the time to give legitimacy to those who were abusing the law. But anyone with experience in totalitarian regimes knows that the law can be changed, it's flexible, it will be used and abused by the authorities to their wishes. Prijedor was not a place where the rule of law was respected. Power came from political power and the barrel of a gun, not from words written in a statute. We know that Dr. Stakic was the president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly, created in January of 1991. The documents would be S6 and S47. We know that he was president of a very important body, in this case -- due to his position as president he became also president of the National Defence Council of Prijedor. And we know he was president of the Crisis Staff, later renamed the War Presidency, but clearly the same body, the same members. Most of the crimes, probably the majority of the crimes that we've talked about in the indictment, were carried out during the period of this Crisis Staff/War Presidency existence. The authority of that body, I think, is best expressed by S109, which was a decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, in which it declared that the Crisis Staffs of the municipality were the highest authorities in the municipality. According to the statute itself or the decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff - it appears in S307. It's also the first decision printed in the Official Gazette in S180 - the Crisis Staff was formed, "To defend the territory of the municipality, ensure the safety of the population and property, establish authority and organise all other aspects of life and work." That is a very, very broad mandate and clearly puts a responsibility on that body for the crimes that were committed. Article 5 of that decision states that the Crisis Staff should "act in accordance with the assessment of the political and security situation." And Article 6 outlines the role the Crisis Staff in the domain of defence of the municipality. If we look just at the legal -- the statutory or decisional authority, as far as the positions and powers of Dr. Stakic, both as the president of the municipal assembly, the president of the Crisis Staff/War Presidency, and the president of the National Defence Council, we can see the importance of his role, much of which is outlined by himself, by Dr. Stakic, at the very beginning of that interview with Channel 4, that interview that appears to have taken place in late December or early January, probably late December, of 1992 because the reporter refers to events in early December. And Dr. Stakic says it's been seven months or more since he took power. That's the video Your Honours have seen many times, portions of it. It's about 45 minutes long. But in the beginning he's asked about what his position is, and he's asked, "Is that like the mayor?" And he says, "Yes, precisely that." We know that the Crisis Staff, the municipal assembly, the National Defence Council would not meet without being convened by the president. It was the role of the president, Milomir Stakic, to convene these bodies. And the witnesses we had from the Crisis Staff or who attended its meetings indicated that their understanding was that they would receive a call from the secretary, who they understood it was the president who had called them indirectly to these meetings. A critical, critical role was that the president set the agenda. Subjects that should have been discussed and were not discussed are the responsibility of Dr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Stakic because he's the one that decided what would be on the agenda. He proposed the agenda for these meetings. Over and over again we've asked witnesses: Why didn't you discuss the crimes? Why didn't you discuss the camps, the disappearances? It wasn't on the agenda. We didn't discuss it. It was Dr. Stakic that set the agenda. And if you look at the agenda of these meetings, you'll see that everything was on the agenda to support the campaign. As I'll discuss shortly, we'll see how often on the agenda disarmament, which clearly was directed to disarming the population that was being targeted to be removed or destroyed, was on the agenda of the bodies headed by Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic told us in S187, in that video, he said it was his duty to sign the decisions. And we've seen that, that he signed the great, great majority of the decisions of the Crisis Staff. And in the gazette, the decisions of the municipal assembly and Crisis Staff, it's indicated that these were -- we have the name of Dr. Stakic SR, signed by Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic presided over the meetings, as he told the journalist. In a response to a question from Your Honours, Mr. Budimir said on page 12919 -- I'm speaking slowly to allow the French interpretation to catch up -- "Mr. Stakic presided over the sessions of the Crisis Staff. He was the one who chaired the sessions, and he was the one who channelled the discussion on various issues that were discussed at the sessions." Every witness who was present at those meetings, who testified, has told us the same thing. The witnesses have also told us, and we've asked how decisions were made, that there was very little formal let's take a vote. The decisions were generally formulated by the president, by Dr. Stakic, and adopted by acclamation. On rare occasions there would be a vote. Mr. Travar, Mr. Budimir both told us that. I believe Mr. Kuruzovic, I believe the same. In his interview, Dr. Stakic said it was his job to implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff. We know that the role of the president of the municipality was a full-time job. The municipal assembly didn't meet daily -- I don't know if we got an estimate, but it clearly didn't meet daily. It met, I'm sure, less than weekly. We have only occasional meetings of the municipal assembly, but somehow those decisions had to be implemented and someone had to coordinate that, and that was why the president was a full-time job. We know that people would come to see him. He had regular meetings. People like Mr. Travar, who headed that very important Ministry for the Economy, control of the budget, told us he would often have to go to see Dr. Stakic. But another critical, critical role of the president of the municipality was that this was the person seen by the public as the representative of the civilian authority. In the videotape S11, Zivko Ecim, before he introduces Dr. Stakic, he introduces him as, "Tonight we have with us the first man in the municipality of Prijedor." In his testimony, Mr. Beglerbegovic, Dr. Beglerbegovic, on page 4084 was asked about whether he heard much about this Crisis Staff. On line 18 he said, "Yes. Most of what was happening in the positions of power was on behalf of the Crisis Staff. Whenever there was some sort of proclamation, it was always by the Crisis Staff. If a rally was organised, if there was a warning, a public warning to the citizens, most of the decisions that were made at the time when the Crisis Staff was founded came from the Crisis Staff or on behalf of the Crisis Staff." He was then asked, "During 1992, did you ever see Dr. Stakic mentioned in the media?" And the doctor answered, "There were a number of such cases in the newspapers, on TV, whenever something was happening, rallies, he was present by virtue of his position because he was the first man in Prijedor. It was logical for him to appear whenever these events were covered in the newspapers or on TV, the radio stations, of course, he was always there." Mr. Murselovic, you recall, who was a deputy for the Party of Private Initiative, he testified on page 2693 of the transcript, line 7, he said, "After the takeover, the Crisis Staff frequently made announcements under that name, the Crisis Staff. They asked the Bosniaks to surrender their weapons. They also asked that the TO posts held by the Bosniak Muslims in villages be turned over as well. They simply issued proclamations through mass media, through radio, and the local papers." It's interesting that when Ivo Atlija from Brisevo testified, at one time he met the bishop, the bishop who was travelling -- the Catholic bishop with Mr. Kupresanin. Mr. Kupresanin was the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Brdjanin was president of the Crisis Staff, but Kupresanin was president of the assembly. And Mr. Atlija asked them for help. He asked, on page 5647, he said, "I asked him again to help us to move out from there and just to go just about anywhere," and that, on page 5648, Mr. Kupresanin told him, "He asked us to address Mr. Stakic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor." We also know how much the press was controlled by the civilian authorities in Prijedor. We saw the meetings of the Crisis Staff National Defence Council how often the Minister of Information and members of the local press Kozarski Vjesnik were present. I recall Your Honour asking Mr. Kuruzovic about the decision of the Crisis Staff, setting the hours of work for the employees of Kozarski Vjesnik. And the Defence made the point, "Well, doesn't the civilian authorities all over the world set the hours for restaurants and catering establishments, as they did in Prijedor?" Well, of course all over the world governments set hours for public establishments, establishments that are open to the public, restaurants or discotheques or -- but they don't set work hours of companies. There's a great difference between setting the hours of public -- when you can have your doors open to the public and telling a company what hours your employees work. The employees of Kozarski Vjesnik wanted to change their hours. If I want to change my hours, I go see my boss, and they did the same thing; they went to the Crisis Staff for permission to change their hours. I think another aspect of Dr. Stakic's contribution to this brutal campaign -- it's a bit subtle, but I think it's not only -- he was in a unique role to contribute to that campaign because he had been, unlike all of the others involved, he had been elected in the 1990 elections. Yes, he had been elected by the municipal assembly to the vice-presidency. No one elected him president. The SDS takeover made him president. But at least among the Serbian population -- and it was so important to this campaign, the brutal campaign against their Muslim and Croat neighbours, that the authorities convince the Serbs of Prijedor, who had lived peacefully for so long together with the Muslims and Croats, to convince them of the necessity, of the righteousness of this campaign, and to the legitimacy of the authorities that were in power. In reality, a one-party dictatorship, the SDS. But in Dr. Stakic they had a person that they could offer as a symbol who had been elected, elected by the assembly to the position -- to the municipal assembly and as the vice-president. We also know that Dr. Stakic in that role as the first man in Prijedor, the head of the civilian authorities, played a very important role in representing these authorities to international organisations. International organisations, reporters, aid workers, didn't go to see Simo Drljaca or Vladimir Arsic. They went to see the president of the municipality. We learned about the ECMM mission to Prijedor, and they met with Dr. Stakic. We know that he gave interviews in the S187 interview to Channel 4 of the British Television, the interview he gave to Monica Gras from the German television. And these are -- I'm now only speaking about international interviews. We know that he was in the centre of the table, he met with that critical, critical delegation that went to Prijedor on the 5th of August with Penny Marshall, Ian Williams, and Ed Vulliamy. And I think one interesting document, it's outside of the indictment period, but it shows the power of the position and the importance in relation with internationals is S9. If that could be put on the screen. Your Honours could take a look at it. I don't know if it's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible to blow it up a little bit. There's a section highlighted which we'll now go to. And this was a article -- can you go back, please. This was an article, "Prisoners in Manjaca should be released on 26 October," that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik. It's Exhibit S9. And apparently, as indicated in this paragraph, this was agreed polling a meeting of a representative of the International Red Cross with Dr. Stakic and associates. Most -- we know that most of these prisoners in Manjaca at this time came from Prijedor, and the issue was whether they'd be released and allowed to go back to Prijedor. We know that they were -- we know from testimony of some of the people that were there that the agreement was that they were released to go out of Bosnia through Croatia and had to agree not to come back. Although, Manjaca was a military prison in Banja Luka municipality, it was Dr. Stakic, the representative, the president of the municipal assembly, and I think the word "mayor," which Dr. Stakic agreed to in his interview is appropriate, the major of Prijedor, was the one who had to give permission for these people to be released on the condition that they not return to Prijedor. Dr. Stakic played a critical role linking the local authorities to the broader republic and regional authorities. In document S93, we see he was elected to represent the Prijedor municipality at the SDS convention, republic level, on the 9th of July, 1991. S99 is a letter from Karadzic to the presidents of the municipality ordering them to set up these 24-hour information centres, if I recall that document. In document S100, we see that Dr. Stakic reported to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly on his meeting with the main board of the party at the republic level. S139, I believe, is a letter in May 1992 to the presidents of the Municipal National Defence Councils, Prijedor, Dr. Stakic, regarding travel permits and implementing work obligations. In S140, we see there's a conclusion of the ARK Crisis Staff regarding collecting illegal weapons and restricting employment to persons absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic. It's addressed at the top in handwriting addressed to the president of the municipality personally. We also see other documents where particular responsibilities and duties were given to the president. In S109, the ARK Gazette decision number 17 on page 29 says that the "Presidents of municipalities should immediately recommend judges and prosecutes for the local courts." Decision number 6 in that Gazette says that the National Defence Council presidents, again in the case of Prijedor, Dr. Stakic, should take immediate steps to disarm paramilitaries. So, Your Honour, what our evidence shows that - and I'll discuss this more after the next break - our evidence shows that the campaign that took place in Prijedor was coordinated among three principal bodies: The military, the police, and the civilian authorities. The centre of that coordination was the civilian authorities. It took place, this coordination, through bodies such as the Crisis Staff and the National Defence Council, headed by Dr. Stakic, presided over by Dr. Stakic, with the agenda set by Dr. Stakic. The public explanations, the excuses for the crimes, the exhortations to people to support an army and police that were committing these crimes, the entire political campaign that was so crucial to the military and police operations were headed by Dr. Stakic. And he, together with the other members of this enterprise, people that you've heard mentioned, such as Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Zeljaja, and Mr. Arsic, carried out this plan, and certainly Mr. Kovacevic contributed. But one thing I'd like to mention about the executive board: First, we know that the executive board was the body that was to implement the decisions carried out by the municipal assembly. So clearly the executive board is subordinate to the municipal assembly and the Crisis Staff, when that existed. There is no doubt that the president of the municipal assembly is superior in fact to the president of the executive board. The most obvious evidence of that is the interparty agreement in Prijedor, as throughout Bosnia, the party that won the most seats, that controlled the assembly, obtained the most powerful position, and that was president of the municipal assembly. We also know from Mr. Travar and from some documents that Dr. Stakic also attended some of the meetings of the executive board when they existed. But it's also important to remember that apparently during this period of the Crisis Staff, when most -- the attack on Kozarac and most of these cleansing operations were taking place and the establishment of the camps, the executive board was not meeting. This is as that body, many of those people were members of the Crisis Staff. In S11 we have the -- it's a television interview with Dr. Stakic, and he says during that interview with Mr. Ecim, "During combat operations, the Crisis Staff existed but the Serb Republic Presidency's decision, renamed the War Presidency --" excuse me. "By the Serb Republic Presidency's decision, renamed the War Presidency, but from the moment real war actions calmed down, we activated the work of the Executive Board," showing, obviously implying, that the executive board was not activated during these combat operations. The Crisis Staff was meeting in its place. This is corroborated by the testimony of Mr. Travar, who said that he objected to the work of the Crisis Staff and urged Mr. Kovacevic to reinstitute the executive board. But just so our position is clear, our position is that Dr. Stakic was superior to the executive board and that during the time when most of these crimes were committed the executive board wasn't even meeting and virtually all of the important decisions that were made, that affected these crimes, were always made by the Crisis Staff. This would be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Only that you know, we may continue now until 1.00, and we'll then move over to Courtroom I because there are some complaints that no public gallery is available for the closing arguments, and so we will do, if possible, also on Monday. Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence in this case shows very close cooperation between the civilian bodies, headed by Dr. Stakic and the army, the army that became -- went from the JNA to the Army of Republika Srpska in the middle of May, 1992. I'm sure Your Honours recall the video S11, in which Colonel Arsic is interviewed, and the interviewer says, "Here we are with the man best informed about events in Prijedor," and Colonel Arsic answers, "It is not only me being the best informed on events in Prijedor. All authorities and their bodies are very well-familiarised with events in Prijedor, and as I, maybe more than others, cooperate with them, I am very familiar." We know that there are many meetings between bodies headed by Dr. Stakic and members of the military. If you recall, it was, according to the testimony of Mr. Kuruzovic, before the takeover it was Dr. Stakic that called for a meeting at the barracks in which Colonel Arsic was in attendance to plan the takeover. We have the minutes of the National Defence Council. We have three of them, S28, S60, I believe, and S90. S28 is the 5th of May, and I believe that's the second meeting. And S60 is the 15th of May, and that's the fourth meeting, I believe, indicating that there was at least one in between. At those meetings Colonel Arsic was there, Vladimir Zeljaja was there, Pero Colic. We also know that there was a call for a member of the garrison to be a member of the Crisis Staff, and witnesses such as Mr. Baltic told us that members of the army regularly attended meetings of the Crisis Staff. Mr. Zeljaja was interviewed in the document S274, a newspaper interview, and he said, "The brigade command was, because of that, immediately linked to the leadership of the SDS, giving them important support, as they do for all decent Serbs, to organise themselves for defence in case of an attack by the Muslim forces." And he was speaking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the period before the takeover when the elected government, multi-ethnic government of Professor Cehajic was still in power. He went on to say on the next page, ending in the ERN number 2749, "I must emphasise here in this region and more or less everyone knows that, the very close cooperation between the army and police. Such cooperation was also established with the leaders of the party, the Crisis Staff, and all decent Serbs who were and still are of importance for this town." Your Honours, we know that in the former Yugoslavia there was a particular philosophy of national defence called All People's Defence, in which the civilian and military were organised to cooperate to the maximum extent possible. And we know that the former Yugoslavia feared invasion by stronger forces and the concept was to have units operating on a local level that could do so autonomously in cooperation with civilians, with the Territorial Defence, the military all working together. All the decisions that we see of the Crisis Staff and the municipal assembly when we look at the events that happened, we see the very close cooperation between the political and the military in Prijedor. So, for example, it was the Crisis Staff that would issue the demands and the threats if you do not disarm, if the weapons are not surrendered, you will be attacked. And in fact, when that didn't happen, they -- the attacks took place. The evidence was, I believe, that there was a 12.00 noon deadline for the surrender of weapons in Kozarac. And I think in the military's own documents it indicates that at about 12.10 or 12.20 - I'm not sure of the exact time - the attack began. I think one example of the cooperation and the interplay, the blurring of lines between civilian and military in the time of conflict, was the document S432. That was the document, Your Honours will recall, a fairly recent document, which indicates in the document that on the 3rd of May the Crisis Staff -- there was an order for uniforms for key political leaders, including Dr. Stakic. And we know that when these uniforms arrived, the members of the Crisis Staff and including Dr. Stakic would wear those uniforms. The testimony of many of the witnesses is that this was mandatory, I think they said, in June. But we have a picture from August when the journalist visited. And you'll recall that you saw the videotape of the visit on the 5th of August of the foreign journalist to Prijedor. And we can show again to remind you, hopefully in a moment, that photograph of Dr. Stakic wearing a uniform, which is now -- should be on your screens. We see him leaning forward in a camouflage uniform with a gun on his right hip. And remember I asked Colonel -- General Wilmot, the Defence expert, how do you distinguish military and civilian? And he answered, "The uniform is the first thing." And here we see that the Crisis Staff was in uniform because in -- in accordance with that doctrine of All People's Defence, the Crisis Staff was part of that military effort, was a key coordinator, supported the military politically and logistically, and in the planning of operations. This was not a case where the 43rd Brigade was fighting in another country or in a front hundreds of kilometres away. In this case, the 43rd Brigade was attacking Prijedor. The people that were the subjects of the attack were the citizens of Prijedor that Dr. Stakic was purporting to represent. So clearly he was informed, and the evidence shows he cooperated in those military -- in that military campaign. I'm not going to go through all the documents, because Your Honours are aware of them, but we know from the evidence and the documents how key the logistics support was of the Crisis Staff and the municipal assembly for both the military and the police. At this time we know that fuel was precious. One of the Defence witnesses said it was more precious than gold. There was an international blockade, trade blockade, against Yugoslavia. The fuel that was reaching Yugoslavia was smuggled in. And the Crisis Staff controlled the distribution of that fuel, made sure that places like the army, that the police and people like the camps at Omarska received the fuel they needed for military operations, fuel that was used to transport prisoners to camps, between camps, fuel that was used and buses from Autotransport Prijedor to not just take people to the camps but to transport tens of thousands out of Prijedor, deported and forcibly transferred across international frontiers and the front lines to areas controlled by the government and Sarajevo. We have decisions showing that the Crisis Staff and municipal assembly assisted with the pay for soldiers, for reserve police. There are decisions regarding the use -- the confiscation and use of illegally acquired material. And if Your Honours recall the decision -- or excuse me, the document S433 regarding the logistics based at Cirkin Polje, it was recently discussed with Major Kuruzovic. We saw that that document which was entitled "Report on mobilisation of vehicles," we saw that in that document - it's on page 5 - it indicates, "We have also provided the weapons and ammunition for sector staffs and secured about 100.000 meals to members of the police and Serbian army TO units." That document shows food for the guards going to the checkpoints, food for the guards going to the camps, logistics support for those that were actually perpetrating the crimes that we heard about in this case. It's never been our position that Dr. Stakic is in the formal chain of command of the army, but we see in the evidence that the lines of authority were blurred and there was great influence of the Crisis Staff and civilian authorities over the army. I'm not going to repeat now what you can read in our brief but even in our 98 bis response on pages 18 and 19 we list 18 decisions directed to the army, decisions such as replacing the logistics commander, the mobilisation commander, confiscating illegally acquired material, continuing the blockade of the town, setting up the intervention, the joint intervention platoon, and the decision that the brigade would provide security at Trnopolje. All of those decisions were carried out. But I think the most telling example of the cooperation and coordination were the demands of the Crisis Staff for the surrender, the threats to attack, and in fact these threats were carried out by the army according to the schedule that had been announced by the Crisis Staff. There was equal or greater cooperation between the civilian authorities and the police, as one would expect. Again, formally, very, very formally, the chief of the police reports, is appointed by the minister in Pale at the republic level, and that is his superior. But the reality of the situation, even before these events, we know that this is a local politician that's normally appointed to this position. All of the witnesses have said that all of the chiefs of police were appointed on the nomination of the local political leaders, the local assembly. No one could give any example in Bosnia of a local police chief selected by the local leaders who had been rejected by the minister. That was a formality. I imagine maybe this occurred at some time if the person lacked a basic qualification or had a criminal record. It's possible. But the practice was this person was nominated by the local politicians and it was accepted by the minister. Mr. Talundzic was not a professional policeman. He obtained the position because as part of the interparty agreement, the winning party, the SDA, was entitled to nominate someone, and they nominated Mr. Talundzic. Mr. Drljaca, similarly, was not a professional policeman. And I'll come to him in a moment. We know that there was a direct phone, one of the witnesses for the Defence told us, between the office of the president of the municipal assembly and the chief of police, the chief of the SUP. And again, we have many, many examples of decisions by the civilian authorities, the Crisis Staff in particular, and the municipal assembly to the police that were carried out. We even have a report from Mr. Drljaca to show -- that shows so strongly how he subordinated himself to the civilian authorities and the Crisis Staff. We have his report sent to Mr. Baltic reporting on the implementation of decisions by the police, the SJB, on the decisions of the Crisis Staff and the executive board how those decisions had been implemented by the police according to those instructions. The Crisis Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Staff, for example, established a curfew. The police enforced the curfew. One of the Defence witnesses - I think it was Mr. Prastalo, the person who was managing Hydrofleks company, came and started - I remember he was saying the civilian authorities had no authority over the police at all. They could not tell the police to do anything. But in his own testimony he told us that his company had been seized following a decision of the civilian authorities that the property had been abandoned. Apparently the owner was a Croat, so the civilian authorities decided to seize it, and the police showed up and implemented that decision. Throughout Prijedor we have many, many examples. It was clear that the decisions of the Crisis Staff were not worthless pieces of paper. These decisions were enforced by the police. And when they were directed to the army, they were enforced by the army. The Defence has raised many times the question of the -- Mr. Drljaca. They talked about Mr. Drljaca's personality. The evidence that we have received in this case makes it absolutely clear that Simo Drljaca was a killer, he was a ruthless killer and a thug. Everyone knew that in Prijedor. Certainly the president of the municipal assembly and the Crisis Staff knew that. It's clear Simo Drljaca was a killer and a thug, but he was Dr. Stakic's thug. They worked together. They complemented each other. They shared the same goals, and each played their own role in coordination in that genocidal campaign that took place in Prijedor. We have the decisions of the election of Simo Drljaca on the 16th of April. That didn't come from the Interior Ministry. It came from the local SDS party or the assembly controlled by the SDS party. They had admitted a few other Serb deputies from other parties, but it was an SDS assembly. Simo Drljaca needed Dr. Stakic. He wasn't a professional. He wasn't elected. He was a political appointee. And when Dr. Stakic lost power, not surprisingly Simo Drljaca lost power. When Dr. Stakic came back to power in 1996, Simo Drljaca came back to power. We've seen a lot of interviews with Dr. Stakic to foreigners and the local press in Kozarski Vjesnik and on television. We've heard people who were present in meetings with him. We've never heard one word that Dr. Stakic criticised the work of Simo Drljaca. Dr. Stakic did nothing to remove Drljaca or to stop him from the ruthless killing that he was taking -- carrying out. And the only logical inference from that is that was what Dr. Stakic wanted. In the interview in January 1993, I believe, with Monica Gras from German television. I'd like to play a short excerpt of that. And I'd ask you to focus on the brief comment that Dr. Stakic makes about the chief of the SUP. Recall this is after the discovery of the camps. This is after thousands have been killed. This at the end -- after the indictment period, following the room 3 massacre, following the Vlasic massacre. Listen to how Dr. Stakic describes the work of Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] People are refugees now in camps, in Germany mostly. If they wished to return, could they now return? In the whole of this war, even if the war is not over yet, it was all about jihad, because the aim of the war was to establish a Muslim state in Europe and the Balkans is part of Europe in geographical terms. Now, how the whole thing will turn out, we'll see. Islam, that is, jihad, won because many Muslims moved out of these areas and went to Germany. Actually, they went all over Europe. Now, why am I saying this? Because all the Muslims from this area were in a position to choose whether they would go to Zenica, Sarajevo, Travnik, or Western Europe, and they opted for Western Europe. They didn't want to leave. They didn't want to even hear about Zenica, Travnik, or Croatia. They didn't even want to go to Croatia because they knew that they were not welcome there. They wanted to go to Western Europe for economic reasons and because their jihad tells them to do so. Let me now return to your question. Regardless of all of this, here in Prijedor what has been done is exactly what the chief of SUP told you. In such a pedantic manner that even some countries in peacetime would be envious of that. About 50 experts worked on this, crime inspectors, around the clock, and we have accumulated so much material so that all those who have blood on their hands will never be able to return. Those others, once the war is over, will be able to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of those would not be able to return because thousands were killed by Simo Drljaca, the chief of the SUP, in the very neat way that Dr. Stakic describes. I think I'd also just like to briefly comment upon the general attitude shown in this brief -- these brief comments by Dr. Stakic towards Islam, comments very -- that remind me very much of the testimony of the Defence expert witness, the paranoia and intolerance towards the religion of Islam that's displayed by Dr. Stakic in this brief interview. In this interview he particularly -- it's interesting he's speaking to a German reporter and trying to provoke, I would say, the prejudice that these -- that the Muslims were bringing jihad to Germany by going there. If Dr. Stakic spoke like that to sophisticated reporters from Germany, imagine how he spoke to Serbs from Prijedor. We know how he spoke to Serbs from Prijedor. He appealed to paranoia. He made historical references to the genocide that did occur, the horrible killings that occurred in World War II, and he portrayed those who were of the Muslim belief. In fact, in Bosnia many of the Muslims hardly practiced their religion. Many of the Bosniaks hardly practiced their religion. But Dr. Stakic portrayed all of them as religious fanatics, zealots, intent on jihad, and a threat to their Serbian neighbours. Stakic spent a lot of time with Drljaca. Drljaca was a member of the Crisis Staff. He was a member of the National Defence Council. Witnesses have talked about seeing them together, seeing Drljaca in Stakic's office, seeing them at restaurants. They may not have been close friends, but they clearly were close associates and worked closely together in this campaign, the criminal campaign that took place in Prijedor. Your Honour, I want to briefly now review these events somewhat chronologically, the crimes, the planning that took place, and then the crimes that were carried out. We know that the plan to take over municipalities, to make them Serbian municipalities, came -- started in 1991. There is the very famous document, the Variant A and B document from the 19th of December, 1991, and there was testimony about that being discussed in the Prijedor local SDS. Mr. Miskovic reported on it. We know that the goal was, as Dr. Karadzic said at that 12th of May assembly, the separation of national communities. From the document S430, which was the interview about -- I believe entitled "Memories of April's events," that we discussed with Mr. Kuruzovic. Mr. Kuruzovic is interviewed and, I forget, but someone is interviewed before him. I forget the individual. But they talk about how separate Serbian police stations were established back in November of 1991 by Mr. Jankovic. We know that the takeover itself was planned in detail in coordination between the police and the army. There's not a need, I think, to play it again, but we have the interviews from S91 on the radio with Simo Miskovic with Slobodan Kuruzovic, with Dr. Kovacevic, talking about the careful planning that went into that takeover. Mr. Kuruzovic -- Mr. Kuruzovic, in S430, the article about the memories of April's events, told us that the timing was moved up. It was originally planned for the 1st of May, and then because of this telegram Dr. Stakic called a meeting at the barracks and the decision was made to move it up, to do the takeover between the 29th and 30th, and in fact in the early morning of the 30th the town was taken over. Immediately upon the success of that takeover, it was reported to Mr. Kupresanin, president of the ARK assembly. Your Honour, the takeover itself is interesting in how it was carried out. The takeover clearly, the 30th of April, was just the first step of the plan because the town was taken over, an area without a large, large Muslim -- certainly there was not a Muslim majority there. Clearly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those planning it wanted to take over the key institutions. And what were they? The police and the municipal assembly. The first person mentioned by the witnesses as being denied entry is Mohammed Cehajic. According to the Defence, he held a position of very little power. But clearly that wasn't true. Clearly those doing the takeover didn't see that. He was the first person, the president of the municipal assembly, that they denied entry to. Because of the overwhelming force that was in the hands of those doing the takeover, there was no resistance, and Prijedor was occupied, the town, but the areas that were predominantly Muslim, Bosniak, and Croat remained in the hands of the local leaders of those communities. People who resisted the takeover, the disposal of the elected multi-ethnic assembly by the authorities representing a single party. And life began to change immediately once the takeover happened. Witness P testified on page 3322 of the transcript. He was asked: "What happened? How did life change for you and for others in the Kozarac area, your neighbours, after the takeover on the 30th of April?" And he answered, "Well, we became prisoners. It became a ghetto in a territory, the telephone lines were cut off from the rest of the world. Physically, we were also cut off because all the roads were blocked. So we felt this insecurity. We felt that we were in some kind of a prison." People from the town talk about dismissals, first of the directors -- first of the political leaders, then shortly after, the directors, people like the director of the SDK, in the hospital, dismissals of doctors at a time when conflict was -- medical care was needed at that time as much or more than any other. But doctors were being dismissed. Although there wasn't an attack in Prijedor town like there was in Kozarac or Stari Grad, in the main town, in areas like the Brdo, Brisevo, Ljubija, life in Prijedor town itself became what Witness Z described on page 7556, "Prijedor itself was like a camp." Other witnesses, doctors, Beglerbegovic, the first witness I talked about who I won't name, talked about that period of time of waiting, waiting for what they sensed, what they knew would be the next act against them. Both of them I eventually arrested; neither of them political; neither of them involved in any politics, certainly not in any military events, but leading people arrested and taken to camps, as were judges, lawyers, leading professionals, many of them women not involved in politics, some of them even married to Serbs, taken to camps like Omarska, once it was established. Your Honour, once the takeover happened and these ghettos were created or these areas that were outside of control were created, it was clear that the plan was never to live like that, for the Serbs to simply allow the Muslims to sit in Kozarac with their own community, in places like Ljubija and the Brdo. Immediately decisions, preparations for conflict, began. And as in most genocides, the first thing you do is ask the victims to please disarm on the order of the authorities, disarm. You know, you're a threat to us if we see you have weapons. So we have decisions from the ARK Crisis Staff, I believe, on the 4th of May instructing the municipalities to order the disarmament of what they call paramilitaries. At the same time we know that the Serbs had been arming, as Dr. Stakic said in one of his interview, arming their own citizens in villages. In the National Defence Council meeting of the 5th of May, point 7 - I think if we can have that on the ELMO -- on the computer screen, S28 - you will see that point 7 of that meeting, just a few days after the takeover, dealt with paramilitaries, individuals possessing weapons in order to surrender them to the police. On S67, there is an order -- this is the order from the ARK that the "Presidents of the National Defence Councils are to report." And again the president in Prijedor was Dr. Stakic -- "to the War Staff of the ARK about actions to disarm paramilitaries." On the 15th of May we have S60, another meeting of the National Defence Council, again in the presence of the military and police, and point 4 again deals with the disarmament of paramilitary formations. Preparations had begun right after the takeover. S345 is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps military. And we see in the highlighted paragraph, if that can be blown up, that on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 105-millimetre Howitzer battery and one Anti-Armour Artillery Battery were relocated from the front in Croatia where there was a cease-fire but no peace to the Prijedor area in order to strengthen the units in the wider Prijedor-Ljubija-Kozarac area. The units have taken up their positions." These are the units that were used to attack the civilian populations of Hambarine and Kozarac just a few weeks later. The Defence would like to rewrite the history to say that the conflicts in Prijedor began with the incident in Hambarine. This was the excuse used by the authorities and promoted by people like Dr. Stakic for the deaths of hundreds and thousands. If you recall the Hambarine incident, first let me say that I don't know exactly what happened in that incident. Clearly there was high tension, a group of Serb soldiers passed along, there was a -- shooting, one Muslim was wounded, two Serbs were killed, the other -- other occupants of the car were wounded, slightly wounded. The closest eyewitness that we have, who was not present during the actual shooting, was Dr. Mujadzic. He talked about treating the wounded, including the Muslim who had a shot in the hip, in the back, consistent, I would say, with someone turning when they saw a gun being pointed or when fire started opening, trying to run. But I do not say that I know what happened, and I would have to say that if -- in our pre-trial brief, if we say that this was a pre-planned provocation, that's overstated from the evidence. But what's clear is the incident was used by the authorities as an excuse for actions that far exceeded anything that could have been justified by what did occur. Remember, even one of the Defence witnesses who testified had passed through that checkpoint that morning, spoken himself to Aziz Aliskovic, had a uniform on and a gun in the car and was allowed to pass by. What did those four or six soldiers in the car do to provoke the shooting? Did they point their guns? Did they first shoot their gun actually at the Muslims first? I don't know. As Dr. Mujadzic said, the situation called for an investigation. What it certainly didn't call for is an attack upon the entire Hambarine region against people who had nothing to do with what happened at that checkpoint. According to Witness DD, when he passed by there were two or three people manning that checkpoint. The Crisis Staff used that incident. And if we look at S389-1, the article from Kozarski Vjesnik, this is an article signed in the name of the Crisis Staff, dated the 23rd of May. And the Crisis Staff wrote, "The Crisis Staff hereby wishes to warn that there will be no cautionary operations in the future, but that the territories where perpetrators of such crimes and members of the paramilitary formations are hiding will be targeted directly." They then ordered the surrender of Aziz Aliskovic and give a deadline of noon on Saturday, the 23rd of May. In fact, we know, I think from the witnesses, that it was about 15 or 30 minutes later that artillery, tank fire was opened from several directions on Hambarine. The Crisis Staff went on to say, "This crime has exhausted all deadlines and promises and the Crisis Staff no longer can, nor is it willing to, guarantee the security of the population of the above-mentioned villages." Your Honour, you don't target a population because a crime may have occurred in an area. You don't target everyone who happens to live in the same town. The Defence witness who testified, Witness DD -- well, let me first point out a few other documents. Excuse me. S152, on page 2, was the report of Mr. Drljaca to the CSB in Banja Luka. And he talked about the events in Prijedor and he said, "Since the residents of the village of Hambarine did not abide by the decision of the Ministry of People's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence of the Serbian Republic --" and that would be in Prijedor at that time, Mr. Budimir's ministry -- "and did not surrender their weapons, refused to cooperate with the legal authorities regarding the attack against the soldiers and rejected the demand set by the army, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality decided to intervene militarily in the village." And then if we go to S240. Okay. Yes, it's now on the screen, S240. The transcript is 1-A, on page 1, line 26. In that -- that's that television broadcast that -- it's one of the tapes that Mr. Sivac brought. And in that broadcast of the Prijedor Television, it said "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality requested the people from Hambarine to surrender, former policeman Aziz Aliskovic and his group, who carried out the attack on soldiers. The twelve o'clock deadline was not observed. Half an hour after the deadline expired, the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina launched an artillery attack at Hambarine and cleaned up the area." How did they clean up the area? Witness DD was a Defence witness, and he told us about how this incident was provoked at the checkpoint by the Bosniaks, by the Muslims. And then he talked about driving through a day or a few days later. On page 9558 he's asked what he saw, and he said, "Well, first of all, houses were destroyed, as I said yesterday. From about the midpoint in the Prijedor field onto the highest peak in Hambarine, mostly to the left and right of the road, as I said yesterday, about between 40 and 50 houses. After several days, I learned that those houses had been shelled by a tank." So that was just from one person driving down that main road, not going off the road. He could see the results of that shelling; 40 or 50 houses from the road visible destroyed, no evidence that these people, these families, had anything to do with what happened at that incident in Hambarine checkpoint. The military's own report - it's even footnoted in General Wilmot's report - indicates that the shelling of Hambarine went on for six or seven hours and witnesses, such as Dr. Mujadzic, talked about the -- how shells were coming indiscriminately at civilian homes, civilian areas. It wasn't a military -- it wasn't an attack on any military operation -- any military target. It was an attack on the people the Crisis Staff had threatened, the people of Hambarine, the Bosniak population of that area. Then in a further attempt to create their own history, Dr. Stakic and his authorities would like to say that Kozarac was a result of a Serb soldier being shot on a convoy, the ambush of a convoy. Stepping back and looking at this in context, we see how ridiculous that was. This shelling of Hambarine happened on the 23rd of May. Negotiations had been taking place. Mr. Kuruzovic was one of those who negotiated. You also heard from Mr. Sejmenovic who was present during those negotiations. The Serbian authorities were demanding that the people of Kozarac surrender to the authority that is had illegally taken power, to the SDS, to the Serbian army that had been created. It was a horrible situation for those people. There was debate among them. Obviously they were out gunned, they were outmanned. But at least a significant section of that population of Kozarac did not want to surrender, and they maintained their positions, their defensive positions, their barricades and dug trenches to defend themselves, arm themselves with what little weapons they had and the very, very slight ammunition they had. We saw that in some of the reports, the 1 KK reports, ammunition that one of the policemen had said at one of these meetings, "We can fire for about five minutes. We've got enough ammunition to last for about five minutes." I don't doubt that a Serb soldier was killed on the approach to Jakupovici, but that was not a convoy that was ambushed. It was an attack. Witness P talked about it, seeing it, seeing the tanks with infantry spread out in what he called "a classical military attack." Samir Poljak lived very close to that checkpoint, and his cousin was at the checkpoint. His family fled, but at one point before his capture, he saw his cousin -- or perhaps it was after his capture - I'm not sure - he saw his cousin and his cousin told him about the attack, how the tanks fired, they returned fire. We know that the resistors were able to damage two tanks. According to the Serb military reports, the 1 KK reports, you'll see that two tank treads were damaged and repaired. Whether that was done with a Zolja, a hand-held rocket, whether that was done just by hitting a trench or by a tree log, it's unclear. It's undoubtable there was some resistance. There's no dispute about that. This case -- it's never been our position that there was not an armed conflict in Bosnian Prijedor. It's an element of our offences. There was an armed conflict. People resisted. And on the 30th of May, one group of people, led by Slavko Ecimovic even tried to counterattack with 80 to 100 men, according to the 1 KK report. There was an armed conflict. That's part of the elements of our offence. Samir Poljak's cousin could not testify because he was taken to the Omarska camp and killed, but he told Samir Poljak that the Serbs opened fire first. And we know that after that, when the tanks approached Jakupovici, almost immediately artillery fire began on the whole area of Kozarac, from several directions, from Mount Kozara, from other areas of Serb villages that surrounded Kozarac, grenades, tank fire, artillery fire, apparently Howitzers were used, targeting the entire area. Shells were falling. I recall -- I'm not going to read it again. I think I read it recently. One of the witnesses -- Mr. Poljak -- Samir Poljak talked about the shells falling everywhere. They seemed to be targeting everyone. People in the fields, houses. Every place. Shells were coming from all directions targeting everyone. There were no military targets there. It was just indiscriminate shelling of the civilian population. Dr. Merdzanic was present in the clinic when this shelling took place. And he was asked about the events that he witnessed, and his attempt to contact the Serbian authorities to evacuate some of the wounded, and I'd like to remind you of his testimony and the response that he received. If we could play that video, which is S -- it's his testimony, the testimony of Dr. Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you treat any children who were injured as a result of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have children who were injured. Some children were wounded during the attack, but we admitted them only the next day, after the clinic had been relocated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had women too, wounded women, but also at the other location, on the following day, while we were still there at the clinic we had another civilian who had been brought in dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that you went to another location on the following day. How did you achieve that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We noticed and were told by the people who had managed to reach us, that it was actually very difficult to get to the clinic. We heard that the majority of the civilian population was afraid and that most of them had left Kozarac and gone to the woods in panic, and this is why we tried to leave that area ourselves. We went to -- towards the Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you establish your second clinic, as it were, the second location of a clinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second location of the clinic was at the outskirts of Kozarac town, on the left side of the main road. It was sheltered by a small wood and a hill. It was housed in a building which was not finished. It was located near a creek. The building itself did not have any doors or windows, but it was naturally protected so that from the direction of Prijedor and from the Kozara Mountain there could be no shells that would eventually hit this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you yourself try and speak to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities in respect of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, we had two children at the clinic who were dying. We were practically unable to help them, and I was very upset by the fact. We had other wounded people, of course, but -- well, at any rate, we were located on the ground floor. On the first floor, there was a police vehicle and several police officers there. They were in contact with the military via radio communication, and I asked whether I could try and negotiate the passage of the wounded, and this is what they enabled me to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police officers, were they Muslim police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were allowed -- or you tried to negotiate the passage of the wounded. Do you know who you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was contacted for that purpose in particular, but the same radio station, the same frequency, was used for that purpose, the same as the one which was used for the purposes of negotiating the surrender of Prijedor and the departure of the population from Kozarac. I think that the contact was -- had been established with the military command that was actually attacking Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you -- the person to whom you spoke, what did you say to him that you wanted to do or wanted to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The surrender of Kozarac, page 25, line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I introduced myself, and I told them that we had two children with us. There was a little girl there whose lower legs, both of them, were -- were completely shattered. She was -- she was dying. And then we had another child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I realise this is distressing for you to recall these events. Perhaps we can just deal with this fairly quickly. Were you given permission to take these injured children out of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I couldn't evacuate the children or the other wounded who were there. The reply we received was not very specific. The only thing they told us is, "Let all of you balija," derogatory for Muslims, "die there. We'll kill you all anyway." So that's what the conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I'd like to play a video of Dr. Stakic talking about the same events, his report from the Prijedor Television about the attack on Kozarac. And that would be S240.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Reporter: The information regarding the fighting in Hambarine, Kozarac, Kozarusa and Kamicani is accessible only through the announcements of the Crisis Staff and the Secretariat for Informing, which are being broadcast on hourly basis on the local radio station. This way the public has been informed that a considerable number of hirelings from the other parts of country, who had already fought in HOS and ZNG have been fighting on the side of Muslim extremists, as well as a number of former officers and non-commissioned officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army who have had the most responsible commanding positions and duties in those battles. The announcements also informed the public that the members of the Green Berets have used all means to force local population into the fight until extinction using the innocent local population, women and children as human shield. The army, however, managed to pull part of population out of the encirclement and house them, and also to put out of the fire, which Muslim extremists had set around their own camp in the Kotlovaca mountain lodge. Once the resistance of the Muslim paramilitaries in Kozarac was quelled, many things became evident and many assumptions came true regarding the long and fateful preparations for the war of extermination, into which Alija Izetbegovic first called up his own people encouraged by the support of the numerous European and world administrators for churning out states. This way several large underground shelters and depots were discovered, equipped with radio stations and supplied with huge provisions of food and beverages, in addition to more than a ton of medications sufficient for one year of warfare have not been on the market for several years. This Crisis Staff has also stated that all the information and documentation found shall be timely announced. With reference to the number of casualties, on both sides they have not been presented yet but it is certain that there were many on both sides. Stakic: Well, I can tell you and the viewers that the whole territory of Prijedor municipality is under our control, which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serbian settlements, and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control since the takeover of power on the 30 April, and now, after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. In Kozarac itself, the operation of "cleaning," as the military call it, is still ongoing because those who have now stayed behind are the most extreme ones and the professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe when we first played this tape we talked about the word used by Dr. Stakic as the word -- the "ciscenje," as the military call it, the cleansing. We saw on that tape the obvious attack upon the civilians of Kozarac. There were houses burning throughout that videotape. We heard from witnesses about what this cleansing operation amounted to. Most of the houses, as you can see, a lot of them are spread out, were not hit directly by artillery fire but were burned, were arsoned after the military moved in. The population wasn't used as human shields by -- as stated in that report but as those who were part of that population testified, they were ordered to surrender and the Serbian authorities divided them, many, especially women and children, were taken to the Trnopolje camp, some through Prijedor, at the sports hall I think they were briefly detained. Men were separated, taken to Keraterm and Omarska. It's also interesting on that videotape to see again the close coordination between the Crisis Staff, Dr. Stakic, and the military operation. He says, "We'd taken power in Prijedor town on the 30th. Now we control the whole municipality." The operation was coordinated, the media announcements, the justification was given by the political leadership, by Dr. Stakic. This political aspect is important because the people of Prijedor, the Serbs of Prijedor, were not any different from people from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, other parts of Europe. It's never been the Prosecution case that there was a genocidal intent by the average Serb of Prijedor. They had to be deceived. They were victims of Dr. Stakic and the political campaign, the media campaign, portraying themselves as being in danger themselves of a genocide. This propaganda campaign, this political leadership, misleading of the Serbian people, paid -- played a key role in the crimes that were committed. I'd like to briefly mention that the crimes, the attacks on areas did not stop with Kozarac. There's also an operation, one of the bigger -- there's several other operations, but one of the biggest was the cleansing of the Brdo region in the -- late July. We heard about that, and we saw a newspaper headline about one Serb soldier, again the same type of excuse was used. There's a newspaper headline "One Serb soldier killed. Army plans ciscenje." And about a Serb soldier being killed in the Brdo region, somewhere not too far from Hambarine. Witness DD for the Defence talked about that, his recollection. He heard two Serb soldiers, I believe he said, were invited in for coffee somewhere and were killed. He didn't know by who, but that's what he had heard. And in response, the army did a ciscenje, a cleansing of Brdo. Brdo was about seven villages. I don't remember all the names but places Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Rakovcani, Carakovo, all those places were cleansed. Witness DD was -- told us he was asked to participate to a limited extent to guard one of the buses. He claimed nothing bad happened on his bus, but he said he was on the second-to-last bus from that area when the cleansing of the Brdo region.
