Several of our witnesses - and I do not recall the names now - talked about all of the killings that happened during that cleansing operation, bodies that were in many, many locations, and how all the men were taken away. Witness DD corroborated that. He was trying to excuse it because of these Serb soldiers who got shot having tea or coffee, but he said he was on the second-to-last bus. They went to Omarska, Omarska was full, and then they were told to go to Trnopolje. And Your Honour Judge Schomburg asked him, "How do you know you were the second-to-last bus? How can you know that?" And he answered, "Because there was nobody left, because everybody was taken from Brdo. We were the last two buses. Every other man had been taken away from those seven villages." The testimony of the Prosecution witnesses, such as Mr. Sivac, corroborates that, that in late July we know that about 20 buses, 12 or 20 buses, came to Omarska. We know from the witnesses who were at Keraterm about these people from Brdo region in late July arriving at Keraterm. Witness B was at least one of those. I recall talking about it. And he talked about the particularly brutal treatment that these young men -- generally young men but men from Brdo received, how they were all packed into room 3, how they were taken out that day, forced to disrobe and engage in some kind of sexual humiliation, pretend that they were having sex with each other, put back in room 3. We know that a machine-gun was set up that day outside of room 3, and we know that throughout the night for hours machine-guns were fired, automatic weapons were fired into that room, killing an unknown number but well over 100, well over 100 of those men from Brdo, massacred in room 3, in Keraterm in front of the guards, the police guards from Keraterm, by a military unit, loud enough, Keraterm being right in the town, on the edge of the town, loud enough for thousands of residents of Prijedor to hear, to know, for word to get out that there had been a massacre in Keraterm that night. Even Mr. Travar who lived nearby talked about hearing the fire for hours. Again, the political leadership tried to mislead and justify crimes like that by pointing to a crime, the shooting of a Serb. It's never been our position that no crimes were committed by other sides. Throughout this war in other regions it's clear - it's the position of the Office of the Prosecutor - crimes were committed by all sides. Even in Prijedor we do not say that no crime was committed against a Serb. That would not be true. But it's not only a principle of international law tu quoque, forgive my pronunciation, but it's a fundamental principle of humanity. You can't kill innocent people in revenge or in response to an act that they had nothing to do with. And that's what was happening in Prijedor. And clearly, given the minor nature of the crimes that allegedly justified these attacks, they were simply -- simply a pretext for attacks that were long planned. The plan was to change forever the demographics of Prijedor, and that's seen in the scale of the crimes, in who was targeted in the crimes, in the destruction of homes so that there would be no place for people to go back to, religious institutions. The -- one of the key aspects of this genocidal plan, of course, were the camps that were set up. And I think Your Honours in one of the questions you asked was -- I forget the exact question -- in the questions you've submitted to us to be addressed in our brief was about whether we equate all of the camps. Obviously the camps were different. They are not all on the same scale. People were not held in the same numbers, for the same duration. And there was a difference between a camp like Trnopolje and Omarska and Keraterm. Trnopolje camp was generally a place -- it was like a place where you herd in cattle before you ship them off, because that's in fact how many of them were shipped off, in cattle cars. It was located a few hundred yards from a train station. People were brought there for the purpose of making sure that they left Prijedor and left Prijedor for good. They had to sign over their property. They left with what they could carry. And most of them gladly left because they were facing the possibility of death if they stayed. I don't call that a voluntary departure. They left because they were threatened. They had nothing left in Prijedor. Many of them, their homes had already been burned, many of them their jobs had been taken; all of them were under terror because of the campaign of killings that was going on in Prijedor, and they left assisted by the Crisis Staff, the one assistance the Crisis Staff and Dr. Stakic gave was to make sure to organise the buses, the trains, the trucks and cattle cars that were used to take people out of Prijedor. But Trnopolje itself was not a nice place. And Your Honours have heard evidence of that. I would like to just briefly, though, remind -- show you photographs that Dr. Merdzanic had given to the foreign journalists on August the 5th. And you see this young man, one of the men he treated in the clinic in Trnopolje. Trnopolje -- and now I'm talking about, of the camps before the arrival of the foreign journalists and before the arrival of the International Red Cross. There was very little food. There was very little hygiene. People dug holes in the ground outside, and I think Mr. McLeod and the foreign journalists -- foreign monitors who visited talked about the extreme risk of disease due to the lack of sanitation. And people, as we see here, were beaten in Trnopolje, people were raped, and people were killed, but not on the scale of Omarska and Keraterm. But this is one of the rooms that were used for interrogations in Trnopolje, a photograph taken by Dr. Merdzanic. The Defence military expert told us that the camps were completely run by the military. The Defence through other witnesses has tried to imply that the camps were completely the responsibility of the police. But, in fact, the evidence is overwhelming that the camps were controlled by the Crisis Staff. They set it up. They administered it through the police, through the help of the army. The army had to provide security at Trnopolje. The army provided the outer ring of security in Omarska. The police were the guards in Keraterm and Omarska. But clearly under the control of the Crisis Staff. And why do I say that? Well, first we have the documents from Mr. Drljaca, where he talks about first his decision setting up the Omarska camp, which I believe is S107. We know that the camp was set up right after Kozarac was cleansed. People started arriving right after that attack. On the 31st of May Mr. Drljaca set out an order talking about how the camp would be administered. And he said the camp was established "in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff." Now, the Defence -- we also have a document after the visit of the journalists, where Mr. Drljaca reports to the CSB in Banja Luka and in which he says that Omarska and Keraterm were set up according to the decision of the Crisis Staff. The Defence would argue that Mr. Drljaca was trying to shift blame. But, in fact, if you look at those documents, he clearly says the police were running the camps. In no way do those documents exonerate himself. And the first one I've mentioned, the 31st of May document, about the establishment of the camp was -- he would have no reason to be covering up his own role. This was dated the 31st of May. It wasn't to any superiors. It was about how the camp would be administered. And he said "in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff." We also have S151. In that document, we -- it's a video. Excuse me. In that video, the reporter indicates that "Colonel Arsic expressly told the press today that the army had nothing to do with the collection centre of Trnopolje and the investigation centre of Omarska. These are under the sole jurisdiction of the municipal civilian authorities ..." Then we have, we recall, the visit of the foreign journalists to the municipal assembly building on the 5th of August. If you recall, the people at that meeting -- the meeting began with Colonel Arsic and others, but particularly Colonel Arsic trying to encourage the journalists to go Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to Manjaca. Why? Well, we heard from some of the witnesses who were transferred from Omarska to Manjaca, that as bad as Manjaca was, where people were kept in horse stables, Manjaca was a hotel compared to Omarska. The military and the people at that meeting, Dr. Stakic was in the centre of the table, Dr. Kovacevic, Drljaca, Arsic, they tried to convince the journalists to go to Manjaca, but the journalists insisted on Omarska. And finally, Mr. Vulliamy testified Colonel Arsic gave up. He said -- told them on the transcript on page 7923, Mr. Vulliamy said -- Colonel Arsic said, "If you want to go to Omarska, these are the people you need to talk to." And Mr. Vulliamy gestured to his right and he said, "That's how Mr. Arsic gestured towards Stakic and Kovacevic." And then the conversation was taken over by Kovacevic and Stakic. They're the people that they needed to give permission for the visit to the Omarska camp. Finally, we have not only Mr. Drljaca saying Omarska is run by the -- established and controlled by the Crisis Staff, Mr. Arsic saying it's controlled by the Crisis Staff, we have Dr. Stakic himself saying that the Crisis Staff controlled the camps. Your Honours have seen this video several times. It's S187. But I want to read the words again, and particularly the question that he was asked about the camps. The journalist said, "Thank you. There have been reports in the British press about the centres of Omarska and Trnopolje and places like that. Do the authorities in Prijedor have any control, or have they had control over places like that? So twice you see the journalist use the word "control." It wasn't a question of just setting up the grounds or the canteen. "Control." And Dr. Stakic answered, "These places, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor." "The reporter: So these three camps, or how are they ...? "Dr. Stakic: Reception centres. "Reporter: ... Reception centres were formed according to the decision of your civilian authorities? "Dr. Stakic: Yes, yes. As I have said, this was a necessity in the given moment." So clearly Dr. Stakic indicates twice when asked about who controlled these camps that these camps were under the control of his civilian authorities. When he goes on to talk about Trnopolje, he says, "Trnopolje was something quite different. Those people had fled from the ravages of war, from the invasion of those extremists, who pushed their own children, women and children, in front of weapons and tried with them to break through, to pull out across Kozara. They are even known to have fired at their own column of refugees in Kozara and so on. And we simply received them down there in Trnopolje in order to supply them with food, for them to get international aid, for transport to be organised for them to places where they wished to go and to protect them against both Muslim extremists and revanchism by members of the other peoples who had lost their closest kinfolk, their dearest, to prevent these revanchist relations and further bloodshed among innocent civilians." Several things in here are obviously deceptions, knowing deceptions by Dr. Stakic. First they set up Trnopolje to give international aid. We know the International Community was denied access to Trnopolje until the visit of the foreign journalists, which I will come to briefly, which happened because of events at a level far above Prijedor. But I see the time is about up. Let me finish this one quick point. He also -- he says that it was provided to give international aid, but the International Community was denied access. He said that people were free -- went there freely, but in fact we have a decision of the Crisis Staff that no individuals could be released from Trnopolje without their permission. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you. Before we adjourn, let me please announce that there will be on Monday a slight change in the schedule. We'll start only at 9.30 and continue until 1.00 sharp in Courtroom II, and then continue half past 2.00 until 5.00 in Courtroom II -- Courtroom I. And the same procedure will take place today. We will resume at half past 2.00 in Courtroom I. The trial stays adjourned until then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. Let us now hear the third part of the closing arguments of the Prosecution. Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We were talking this morning about the detention camps in Prijedor and the fact that these camps were controlled by the Crisis Staff by the bodies of authority headed by the accused Milomir Stakic. The evidence we have shows that the logistics for those camps were provided by the Crisis Staff. It shows the orders for establishment were done by the Crisis Staff. S84, if we could have that document on the screen, is yet another -- more proof of the knowledge and intent of the Crisis Staff and Dr. Stakic in setting up these camps. This is a decision signed by Dr. Stakic from the Crisis Staff, and it indicates in paragraph 1 that "All businesses, enterprises, and communities are ordered to terminate the employment of those currently in Omarska and Keraterm." A document Your Honours are well familiar with is S110 or 316. I believe it appears twice. And that document provides - if we can have it blown up, the particular paragraph - this is the confirmation document indicating that the conclusion of the 2nd of July, forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm. Excuse me. What this document is is a report on the implementation of Crisis Staff decisions and orders to the police. And one of the conclusions listed is the conclusion regarding forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm. So again, this shows the police obeying the orders of the Crisis Staff who were the ones holding the keys to the prisons, the concentration camps at Omarska and Keraterm. We heard testimony from some of the witnesses of the kinds of people that were taken to these camps, not just those who happened to live in the areas where the ciscanjes were conducted, the largely Muslim, Bosniak, or Croatian communities, places like the Brdo or Kozarac. We know that people from the town, professionals, were taken, people with no connection to any paramilitaries, people without any connection to national parties, people like Mr. Murselovic, who headed an independent multi-ethnic party, the Party of Private Initiative. Judges, women, we heard about disabled persons, persons who could not take part in combat. We heard about one prosecutor who was practically blind, who would have to be led around, put his hand on the shoulder of the -- of someone else in order to go to the meal of the day to find his way. We know that they came for people such as doctors, dentists, judges, and women who were held at the camp. We asked one of the witnesses, Witness B, about the presence of elderly in the Keraterm camp, and I would like to remind Your Honours of his testimony so long ago. But if we can just look at this brief clip of what Witness B told us. And just again for the booth, we're waiting for the clip of the testimony of Witness B. I don't know if there's a problem. If they could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. signal -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're getting no sound. I don't know if we can try again, but we're getting no sound. If we could rewind to the start and perhaps see if we can get sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to move quickly so we can finish your testimony, but I want to ask you:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the camp, were there women that you saw in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no women, except -- well, women did come. They would leave women at the camp, those who were waiting for some transport or vehicles to transfer them to Omarska. Two women even spent the night in our cell. But as a rule, they didn't stay there for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there minors, people under 18 or even under -- well, were there people under 18, minors in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. I even met a boy. He introduced himself to us. And through our conversation he said that -- in the conversation he said that he was 14 years old. You could see that he was a child, but we were really amazed that -- when we heard that he was so young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any people that were older, past the normal retirement age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were older people there, much older than retired people, because I think you could go and retire after -- once you were 60. But there were people who were much older than that. There was even a person who we thought perhaps was even over 70 years old. This was an old man from Kozarac. He wasn't very tall, but he was quite fit and you could see that he was healthy, he was alert. And every morning when we would get up, he would do some exercises, which we found a little silly at that time because he was the only one who did that. But he happened to be the oldest amongst us. So while we were talking to him, he even told us that I -- that he was in Hitler's camp. That's what he told us. He said, "I was in Hitler's camp too, during World War II." So then we asked him, "Which one is worse?" And he laughed and he said, "This one is 100 times worse," because he was in Germany in a labour camp, and he said, "Nobody beat me. I had food to eat. I had my own bed." So he said that this one was much, much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we heard many witnesses from the camps talk about horrific, horrific events that it make sense now to recall the events that happened in the camp. The number of tortures, killings, and the sexual assaults that took place. But I think it's important sometimes to reflect and to see from an individual what that was like, and I recall when we were in this very courtroom the testimony of Samir Poljak, who was asked about just in this brief clip I'd like to play, about his first ten days in the Omarska camp being held in a garage that summer in Omarska. So this is the testimony, a brief clip, of Samir Poljak talking about those first days. Before we start, I'd also like to remind you Samir Poljak came from Kevljani. And one of the witnesses for the Defence talked about Dr. Stakic having worked as a doctor in Kevljani, about how Dr. Stakic was well treated and well -- according to the witness, well loved by the people, the Muslim community village of Kevljani. It's not going to be on this tape, but we know from his subsequent testimony Mr. Poljak's father was killed in this camp, his cousins were killed, and he lost, I believe, his uncles from Kevljani, all from Kevljani. And here he's just describing the first ten days in the garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what the conditions were like in that garage that you were kept in in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just an ordinary garage, as far as I could notice, for cars to be kept in, and that's where they put us, all of us. There must have been around 150, 160 of us or whereabouts -- or thereabouts. So there was not enough room inside this garage for us to sit down. We were all standing from that moment on, like sardines, packed like sardines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in that garage with the group of about 150 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent about ten days there, ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dreadful. When they shot us up, inside it was very hot. There wasn't enough air. I remember that within half an hour or one hour I was soaking with sweat. Everything I was wearing, my shirt, my trousers, it was all soaked in sweat. It was unbearable. I remember that I pressed my hand against the wall and I saw that the paint on the wall began to melt. The ceiling was full of drops of sweat. Sweat was dripping from the ceiling. And then someone -- someone asked to have the window opened. I think someone did. I have no idea. But I remember that someone jumped up and smashed a window in order to get some air inside the room, but that didn't improve the situation because even after that, it was very stuffy and very hot. We asked for water because we were parched, and they said, "Okay, we'll give you some water, but first you have to sing a song." So we sang at the top of our voices. And then a jerrycan filled with water was brought to us and then people started fighting over the jerrycan. It was awful. It was a fight to survive, as simple as that. No one really cared about the person next to them. We fought like animals over the water they had brought us. It was really awful. I remember the first evening two young men suffocated. I remember them very well. They were just lying there on the floor. They were dead. No one flicked an eye. No one paid any attention. That was the state we were in. And everyone just looked after himself. No one had any sympathy for the dead body lying there. Until a day ago, we were still talking -- we had still talked to each other, and now this person was dead. But it made no difference. It was really awful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in those ten days, were you fed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived on Friday, and they gave us nothing until Sunday. They only threw jerrycans of water into the room. And then on Sunday I remember clearly they opened the door and threw in some bread, and then there was chaos because people started struggling for that bread. Everyone was trying to get to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the two bodies, those that had died the first two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bodies were taken out and put on the grass there. I remember the following day or perhaps after two days they gave permission to go out to that lawn one by one so we could take a leak, and when I came out, I saw one of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those dead lads lying there on the grass. How many days had elapsed in the meantime? Two or three days, perhaps. I can't remember. But I saw his body there on the lawn. I remember clearly what he looked like. He was -- he was bigger than me. He was quite tall, and he had curly hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you arrived Friday night. When was it that you were let out of the room for the first time to urinate on the grass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the next morning, but it was -- it was either Saturday morning or Sunday morning. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what you felt like when you were out there and saw the grass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was perhaps 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning. It was a sunny day. I felt wonderful. The smell of the air was somehow pleasant and the sunshine. It was nice. It's beyond words. It was a wonderful feeling. That was something. It stuck in my memory, the morning and the grass, the smell of fresh air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How had your life changed from one week earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unimaginably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Samir Poljak was in high school and was at home when the shelling started in the Kozarac area, and his father was taken from the camp and he's never found out what happened to his father. Your Honour, we cannot understand what happened in Prijedor without knowing about the events of the 5th of August and the visit of the journalist, the foreign journalist, to Prijedor. The events that we've talked about and most of these killings, everything I've mentioned in my argument so far, happened, that military attack on Hambarine began on the 23rd of May and the journalist visit was the 5th of August. The Omarska and Keraterm camps were set up after the attack on Kozarac at the very end of May. So we're talking about a very short period of time; basically June, July, and a few days in May and August. Thousands of people had been killed in that time, and the world didn't know about it. The International Red Cross was denied access to Omarska, to Trnopolje, to any of these camps. In a small town in Bosnia, that certainly I and most of the people had never heard of, Prijedor. There was impunity because the people in power, Dr. Stakic and the others, controlled the press, they lied to their own people, and the world didn't know what was going on. But somewhat as a matter of chance, of fortuity, we know that these events, this incredible visit, started with an interview of Dr. Karadzic in London. A few days before his interview - and all this is contained in the testimony of Mr. Vulliamy - a few days before Dr. Karadzic's interview, articles had been published, second-hand accounts, that atrocities and terrible things might be happening in Trnopolje and Omarska, published by Roy Gutman man and another journalist. During the interview with British Television, Dr. Karadzic was asked about it, denied the charges, and said, "Of course this is not happening. If you'd like, come and see how we treat our prisoners. We don't treat them the way the Muslims are treating the Serbs. The Serbs are being treated inhumanely. You should visit those prisons." On the way -- while Dr. Karadzic was driving to the airport that day or the next day, ITN contacted Dr. Karadzic and said, "We accept your invitation. We have some journalists who would like to go to Prijedor and see these camps." Put on the spot, he said, "Sure, this will be arranged." At that time you could not travel directly to Republika Srpska. The journalists flew to, I believe it was Budapest, from Budapest they drove to Belgrade, and they arrived in Belgrade, I believe, around the very beginning of August, the first day or two. In Belgrade, one of the members of the presidency of Republika Srpska met them there, Nikola Koljevic, the professor of Shakespearian literature. Nikola Koljevic spoke to them and again encouraged the journalists to visit camps where Serbs were held by Muslims, by Croat forces. And again let me reiterate, Your Honour, these claims that Serbs were abused in camps by Muslims and Croats are certainly not disputed by the Office of the Prosecutor. We've even brought cases this is true. Mr. Vulliamy, in fact, and the other journalists took up an offer Nikola Koljevic to visit some camps in Serbia, where individuals were held, and they did visit those camps and they said while it was not a great place, these were not inhumane, you know, violations of international law camps. The camps were not shocking in Serbia. But they kept reiterating, "We want to see Omarska. We want to go see Trnopolje." The journalists had never heard of Keraterm. There were no published reports about Keraterm. And that was not mentioned. Eventually, I think it would be approximately the 3rd of August -- the 2nd or 3rd -- the journalists went to Pale, where they met directly with Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Karadzic again encouraged the journalists, "Please go to Sarajevo and see the places where Serbs are being abused by the government of Alija Izetbegovic and his forces." The journalists explained, "It would take a long time to cross the lines, and, you know, the world is wanting to know about Omarska and Keraterm. We can do you a favour -- Omarska and Trnopolje. Excuse me. We can do you a favour and clear your name. Please let us go to Prijedor. We'll send our colleagues to Sarajevo." And Dr. Karadzic kept telling them, "But you could be in danger." He said, "Journalists are killed all the time and the Muslims -- by Muslims and they blame the Serbs. It will be dangerous for you." The journalists insisted, "We want to see Prijedor." He said, "Please there are some camps here that you can see." And they were taken to a camp in Pale where Muslims were held. And again, it was not shocking. It was a detention facility. People were held under less than ideal situations, but not shocking concentration camps like Omarska and Keraterm turned out to be. Finally they were granted permission and they were sent to Banja Luka. They spent the night of August the 4th in Banja Luka and they were given an escort. A major, I believe his name was Milutinovic, a major on the staff of General Talic to escort them to Prijedor. That was the August the 5th, and that is an incredible day in the history of Prijedor, in this case, because unknown to those journalists, the room 3 massacre had happened about ten days earlier. They were not asking about Keraterm, but everyone in Prijedor knew about the massacre in Keraterm. Despite the attempts to delay the journalists, the attempts to dissuade them, to tell them that their lives were in jeopardy, the journalists persisted that they had to see the camps, and so eventually they were given a sanitised -- extremely sanitised version of Omarska and Keraterm -- and Trnopolje. But it's very interesting. We know that the preparations in Prijedor began before the journalists arrived. We have an order from General Talic to the military saying he received an oral order to allow a foreign delegation to go to Prijedor, make sure the conditions were okay. We know from a witness of the Court - I forget if that witness is protected – (redacted), that she was contacted by Simo Drljaca about a week before the visit and told that foreign journalists would be coming, I will need you to interpret, I'll call you when they come. And what were the preparations that were done? Well, first of all, the Keraterm camp was closed on the 5th of August. That morning the place where the biggest massacre to that date had happened, widely known in Prijedor, was closed, was shut down. The journalists didn't know about it, and the plan was not to let them know about it. Also we know that the trip of the journalist, that they were given very, very little access, especially to Omarska. The authorities knew how much there was to hide in Omarska, so all they were given was a chance to glimpse a kitchen, a cafeteria, people marching in, eating soup. According to some of the witnesses, one of the better soups. It had a few beans in it, and marching out. They were denied any possibility to see the places where prisoners were kept. They were only tried -- the attempt Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was made to have them interview one prisoner that had been selected who understood very well, a very intelligent man, what it was he was supposed to say, and that if he didn't say it, he would be killed. They declined that offer to interview that particular prisoner, who was a witness in our case. Only the Serbian TV that was along with them interviewed that prisoner. Also, in preparation for that visit, it is not a coincidence that that morning one of the prisoners from the Omarska camp was taken out of the camp. If we could see S378, please. We've heard a lot in this case about one individual, Dr. Esad Sadikovic. I believe, Your Honours, although it's always important to put a face - we looked at that book of missing on thousands of dead - to put a face and a personality behind a few of them, Dr. Sadikovic's importance goes beyond just an example of one person who was killed. It's very significant to this case what happened to Dr. Sadikovic and the day that it happened. On that day we know he was taken to the Omarska police station. This record found in the Omarska police station corroborates the testimony of many of the witnesses who said that he was taken out of the camp that day. Why was it so important to keep Dr. Sadikovic away from the foreign journalist? First of all, Dr. Sadikovic had worked for the United Nations in many countries. He was a person who was not a member of any national party. He was married to a Serb. He was a Bosniak by ethnicity but married to a Serb. He was the leader of a peace movement. The Defence witness Marjanovic talked about that, Dr. Sadikovic leading a peace movement. We know from many witnesses that he went around the town trying to avoid conflict, trying to talk all sides out of confrontation. He spoke English. Your Honours, we know that after these small pictures of the Omarska camp were published around the world, the few photographs that Dr. Merdzanic had bravely, bravely given to the journalists, smuggled to the journalists, that we saw earlier of the beaten body that, this had a tremendous effect. We know that the world press descended on Prijedor the next few days. Can you imagine what the effect would have been if Dr. Sadikovic had been allowed to speak to the journalist? It's very difficult to speculate historically, but I wonder what would have happened in the conflict in Bosnia if Esad Sadikovic, who according to all of the witnesses was such a charismatic man, a man of such obvious neutrality in the conflict, and a person who was married to a Serb, had no national agenda, a humanitarian, had worked for the United Nations, what if he would have been on CNN, on the world media, speaking about the Omarska camp? Would the world attention have focussed on Prijedor? Would the war have happened in the same way it did? It took three more years and the massacre of Srebrenica for the world to really focus on the war on Bosnia. The little that was published had a tremendous effect, and it's not because of what was said. It's very much because of what was not said. I'd like to show a few brief clips of what was broadcast, S329. I have a short clip of that. And I think this is actually from two different exhibits, but two short clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Inform anything about the conditions in which you are being kept here, or is it difficult? I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that. You know, I -- can you understand me? Before, it was once upon a time, once upon a -- once in a day, before, in the former camp. I don't know. I just came here. We just came here today. Have people here been beaten? Here? No. Here, no. Not here. In other places? I rather wouldn't talk about that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could stop just for a moment that young man, I have no idea who he is, but he obviously came from Keraterm that day. Whether he was one of those who on the 21st of August, 16 days later was on the convoy to Vlasic, I don't know. What he didn't say had tremendous effect, the way he said it -- they're not -- "Are there beatings here?" "No, not here." And then there's a very brief clip of Dr. Merdzanic being asked similar questions, if this is from S323. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have there been any cases here of people who have been beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the world saw very little. The broadcast grossly underestimated the terror that was going on in those camps, what we now know. The events of that trip did not end with just the closing of the Keraterm camp, because when the camp was closed, the prisoners were divided into three. A group was sent to Trnopolje; among that, that young man at the fence being among them. A group was sent to Manjaca. And first, that morning, the 5th of August, the camp commander read out a list of 120 names. And the testimony of Witness B, those people were loaded on to buses from Autotransport Prijedor, escorted by the intervention squad, a squad that had been in that camp before, beating prisoners, taking away prisoners who didn't return. One of our witnesses recognised, in fact, Dado Mrdja, as giving orders as the prisoners were lined up. 120 of them were put on two buses that morning. We know that those buses went to Omarska and the prisoners spent the night either on the buses or somewhere in the camp. And that very early -- very late that night or very early the next morning, on the 6th of August, an order came from a member of the Crisis Staff, from Simo Drljaca, with a list of 125 names, including the 120 from Keraterm and other names, including Dr. Esad Sadikovic. That was an execution order. They were taken away. They've never been seen alive again. There's one site just beyond the borders of Prijedor municipality in Sanski Most called Hrastovo Glavica where about 126 bodies were exhumed, and I believe one was identified as coming from World War II. So 125 bodies were found there. All of the people identified were identified as being from the people of Keraterm, from that group of buses. Those -- there were a few identifications of DNA, all of them from those people. Again, why was it necessary to kill Dr. Esad Sadikovic? First I'd like you to play -- I'd like to play a short video putting together what three witnesses said about Dr. Sadikovic, two of them from the Defence. The first two are Defence witnesses. Excuse me. Before I begin, I'd also like to remind you the first time I heard the name -- that we heard the name was Witness A who talked about Dr. Sadikovic. He said that he was an incredible man who kept up the morale of the other prisoners and recounted that he treated them one -- even there were head wounds where the scalp was split and there was no needle and thread to sew. He said Dr. Sadikovic braided the hair together to keep the wound -- to keep the two sides of the wound together. He told us a story about how there was one father and son in the camp, and the -- every day Dr. Sadikovic was popular with the guards. He was one of the few people who had the privilege to move around rooms. Everyone liked him. And this father took advantage of it to save a piece of measly bread ration to give to his son who was sick and he asked every day Dr. Sadikovic to carry it. And Witness A told us that one day Dr. Sadikovic was unusually depressed for him and they asked him what was the matter and he said that this son had died and the father gave him the bread and he didn't know what to do with it. And I think he said -- Witness A told us that Dr. Sadikovic offered the bread to all those other hungry men, but no one would eat it. If we could now play the tape. These are, again, two Defence witnesses and one Prosecution witness talking about Dr. Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that Dr. Esad Sadikovic disappeared and is no longer among the living? I think as a colleague of yours, you have given some thought to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, I will explain. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic was a colleague of mine and also a friend of mine. We visited each other. He was my friend. He was a joker, and he was a very professional skilful doctor. I don't even want to think about his possible crimes. And as of his disappearance and of his tragic lot, I can only say that this has -- had a huge impact on me and I feel -- still feel the sadness for the fact that he's not amongst us, that I don't have the opportunity to be friends with him any longer. I simply was not in the position to help him in any way. I was not in the position to find out where he was at the moment when he disappeared, nor what happened to him. All the information that I have about his lot, I -- I had after the war. Dr. Sadikovic disappeared. I don't know when. I can only assume that it was at the beginning of the war. But to -- but to this very day it will happen to me that I see somebody who looks like him and I will hope that it will be him because we were not just colleagues. We were really good friends. So I always mistake other people for him, wishing that it was him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I remember. We were on our way back from the village and we were standing outside the village after the takeover. Esad Sadikovic arrived and Mico was very fond of this man because they were alike, they were people who had a lot of things in common. So Sadikovic came up to Mico him and said - I'll try to quote him - "You know, those idiots of mine over there in that village, those fools" - I'm not from the area, so I didn't remember the village - "they're creating problems again. They set up a barricade. Let's just go there and talk to these people, for God's sake." Mico, without saying a single word, joined Eso. They drove there in a jeep. They stayed there for a long time. It was almost midnight, and Mico still hadn't come back. I was already scared because I did hear a number of things about Eso, a number of things were being said about him. I wasn't sure, but I had seen him before with other Muslims who insisted on ethnic divisions at the time. And Mico -- the sort of person that Mico believed Esad Sadikovic to be was not exactly how he struck me, but I said, "Okay, if Mico had faith in him, then it must be all right." And just before midnight he came back home. I said, "What did you do there?" And he said, "Well, we sat down with those people, we talked to them, we had brandy together and that's how the whole thing ended."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of times in your testimony, Dr. Esad Sadikovic who treated you and treated Mr. Smail Duratovic, do you recall the last time that you saw Dr. Sadikovic? First, can you tell us what kind of a person was Dr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To talk about Prijedor, the town, to talk about these camps, the tragedy, and to omit the name of Dr. Eso Sadikovic would be a sin. He was a deeply humane person, and he helped everyone, whatever their religious background or colour of skin. He was a UNHCR expert, and he had spent a long time working somewhere in the Pacific, in Libya, in a number of African countries helping people. He was a charismatic person in the town of Prijedor. He knew it and he was proud of it. In the Omarska camp he did his best to help whoever he could. And where no one was willing to go and to help, he was always there to do it. He was even helping Serb guards there who would come to -- to take up their shift. They were dead drunk and sometimes they were wounded and they had skirmishes among themselves and they quarreled over money and how to distribute the money they had looted. And he helped them too. And after most of the Prijedor doctors -- or at least, those who were in the camp, had been killed, the authorities in Prijedor knew very well that a finishing touch was to be added. I'll never forget that night because that was the last night in the Omarska camp. It seemed a quiet night at first, but just before dawn broke, a guard appeared at the door and he said, "Dr. Esad Sadikovic, come out and take your stuff with you." We were surprised because we knew that his name had been called out very often, but this time they told him to -- to bring his stuff, so we knew where they were taking him. Dr. Eso stood up. He took his nylon bag in which he had a handful of cigarettes that the other prisoners had collected for him. He brought his dirty shirt and he headed for the door. We all stood up, we stood quietly, and then all of us started -- all of us spoke out loud and he said -- and we said, "Dr. Eso, thank you. Thank you so much for everything." He just turned back. And he said, "Thank you, friends." We did -- and goodbye. We did not believe that there was such -- such a criminal person in this world who would be able to kill a man like Dr. Eso.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour asked Dr. Iglic why, why would someone kill Dr. Sadikovic. And I believe the answer was Dr. Sadikovic was the most dangerous Bosniak to the authorities in Prijedor. He didn't have a gun. He didn't have a military. He had moral authority. He was married to a Serb and he could have swayed the Serbs in Prijedor. He was well loved. He could have swayed the world community because of his complete moral authority, a former doctor for the UN, a medical professional, a colleague of the accused, Dr. Stakic. The idea of a multi-ethnic Prijedor was what threatened the authorities and the SDS. No one impersonated that better, embodied that more than Dr. Esad Sadikovic. The visit, the glimpse into Prijedor that the foreign journalist got, was enough to change the history of what was happening in Prijedor. Keraterm was closed when they were on their way, but immediately after these few photographs were published, the Omarska camp was closed. First, of course, it was turned into the Motel Omarska for a few weeks, beds were brought, most of the prisoners shipped out, and a false Potemkin in Omarska was set up, a false little village. And the killing stopped. When we talk about the ability of the authorities to control the killing, this shows more than anything how much authority they did have. The camps were closed. In Prijedor, the killing stopped, with one exception; that being the largest massacre of the conflict, the massacre over Vlasic Mountain at Koricanske Stijene. This occurred on the 21st of August, but it's not by coincidence, Your Honours, I propose, that this did not happen in the territory of Prijedor. The intent to kill in Prijedor was still there, but so were the eyes of the world. One more killing was planned and this killing was to take place as far away from the world press and the eyes of the world as possible. Your Honours heard the testimony of one of the survivors -- actually, we had evidence of two survivors, one by 92 bis. If we could show S246. We have a couple of photographs. I'm not going to go over in great detail the horrors of that crime because Your Honours have, I'm sure, heard it and we cannot forget it. On that convoy thousands -- there was a thousand or so people, far from Prijedor, near the front line, very close to the front line, past Skender Vakuf, the intervention squad who was escorting the convoy separated the men. Most of those were men that came from Trnopolje. Many, if not most, were former inmates of the Keraterm camp. They were put on -- crammed onto two buses to complete capacity, well over 200, and taken to the side, to this little road, ordered to keep their heads down and march to the side of this cliff, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where fire was opened on them, automatic weapons, where they were machine-gunned and thrown to their death over this cliff, except for several who miraculously survived. Was this crime intended by the authorities in Prijedor? Was the room 3 massacre intended? We know that the massacre of Dr. Sadikovic and the 120 men was intended because we know there's an order from Simo Drljaca. The evidence, the clear evidence that this was intended, is that absolutely nothing was ever done to identify the perpetrators. Obviously if you are those, the ones giving the order, you don't want the perpetrators, those who were carrying it out, identified. Room 3 massacre occurred over hours. There were many guards in the camp. There was a unit of the army, widely, widely known in Prijedor, no one ever arrested or investigated. Vlasic Mountain, we know that a squad of the police, the intervention squad, was sent to escort that convoy, dozen or so men, to go from Trnopolje and Tukovi, where this convoy began, to the front line at Smetovi and back was more than an all-day journey. I believe the massacre happened close in the late afternoon. The convoy started in the morning. The buses stilled that to go back. Would there be records of the unit that was sent to escort that convoy? Of course there would be. Of course the commanders knew who it was. Of course Dr. Stakic, if he had wanted to, could have asked, requested, demanded the records of who it was that escorted that convoy. It isn't just a failure to punish and prevent. It's clear from the absolute lack of efforts that it was intentional, it was ordered. The crimes were carrying out the intent of the authorities. One of the Defence witnesses who testified - we'll not further identify to protect him - showed us a record. One of our documents was a record. It wasn't from the indictment period, but just as an example, of a duty roster of the police that was seized by the OTP in -- I'm not sure, 1997, something like that, showing where every officer was assigned that day. Clearly such records existed for the convoy that went to Vlasic Mountain, for the squad of police from Prijedor that escorted that convoy. Clearly those records would have existed of what army unit was Keraterm in room 3. Remember that Sarajevo Radio broadcast the massacre, the fact that people showed up in -- in Travnik missing over 200 -- 250 relatives missing. It was broadcast the next day. Dr. Merdzanic talked about how people in Trnopolje had listened to the radio. Penny Marshall had given him a radio on her second visit. And there was another convoy scheduled for that day, and the people were afraid to get on it, and Slobodan Kuruzovic, camp commander, assured them that it was okay, that what happened is that the Muslims had shelled this -- this convoy over Vlasic but it would be safe now. No effort was made, absolutely none, to identify the perpetrators, because they were carrying out the intent of the authorities. You don't have crime after crime, tens, hundreds, and thousands killed with no attempt to stop it unless it is because those who are in power want that result, intend that result. If we could have S281-3 put on the computer screen for just a moment. Your Honour, this was a list, I believe -- this is from Nicholas Sebire's report, and it's a list of court declarations of death according to when the person was known to have been killed or missing. At that time of his report there was 900 or so records that were in his database. We see that the crimes escalated, reached their peak in July, but May, June, July, and then last for August. The reason that that happened is the visit of the journalists. When the eyes of the world focussed on Prijedor, the genocide could no longer be carried out. It no longer was in the interests of the Republika Srpska and the political agenda to have the world know what was going on in these brutal, brutal detention camps and the massive, massive killings that were taking place in Prijedor. I believe the evidence shows that those journalists saved thousands of lives, those people who were in the camp and released because of that visit. Your Honour, the scale of the crimes in this case remove any doubt about the knowledge of the accused. If we could show the short video, S326 for just a moment. Whole sections of Prijedor were completely destroyed. We saw some of that in the earlier video where Dr. Stakic was being interviewed while homes all over Kozarac were burning. This is a short ABC Nightline, I think, video driving down the main road, the one that Dr. Stakic would have taken from Omarska to - I believe it is - the road from Omarska to Prijedor. If we could play this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We visited the ethnically cleansed Kozarac in Northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia, restricted to just a few blocks of the town, once home to about 15.000 Muslim women, men, and children. Today there are no Muslims there, none, and none of their X-marked homes is intact. Other homes in Kozarac have been marked to survive. This one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says, "This is Serbia." They stand undamaged like the remaining Serb residents of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe that may have been inside the town. But we also have some photographs taken from by Mr. McLeod on the road, just the road between Banja Luka and Prijedor, which would have been the road travelled between Omarska and Prijedor. And if those could be put on the. These are just individual shots taken by Charles McLeod, the ECMM monitor, as he drove through that destruction in 1992. This is 186-2. We can -- I believe there's -- how many photos? Five photographs, we'll go through them, S186-2, is 168-3, 168-4, 168-5, and 168-6. We know that Stari Grad, an old historical part of the town, was razed to the ground, the two mosques destroyed, all the houses destroyed, except for one house that a Serb happened to live in. We know from the witnesses that virtually every church and mosque was destroyed in the municipality, certainly in Prijedor and Kozarac, the main church in Prijedor, the main mosque in the town of Prijedor were both blown up and destroyed. We know from a record of the Serbian Red Cross, one that was used during the testimony of cross-examination of Mr. Kuruzovic, 23.000 persons according to the Serbian Red Cross went through Trnopolje, 23.000 people. That's about half of the entire non-Serb population prior to the conflict. We know that the demographics of Prijedor changed so dramatically that it went from the Muslim population went from 49.000, approximately, in the 1991 census, to about 6.000, according to an article published in Kozarski Vjesnik in 1993. The lines of women desperate to leave Prijedor would be in front of the SUP building, just across from Dr. Stakic's office. Your Honour, we believe we have shown in this case clearly that the accused had effective control over the perpetrators of this crime, the police and army. He was wide -- the number one man in Prijedor. He appeared often in the media. He had direct contacts with the highest authorities, including the president. We have communications to him from the president of Republika Srpska, direct contacts with Vladimir Arsic and the command of the 43rd Brigade. Never did he denounce or make any effort to stop the crimes. The police and army were dependent upon Dr. Stakic and the Crisis Staff for logistics support, for political support. They always got it. He could have controlled them. He could have disbanded the intervention squad. He could have called for the arrest of people like Dado Mrdja, who were notorious criminals. He could have disbanded the intervention squad. He could have closed the Omarska and Keraterm camps, which he himself has said was set up on the authority of his civilian authorities. We're not saying that Dr. Stakic knew of every single crime that happened. Of course that's not true. But the impunity that reigned in Prijedor because of his rule facilitated those crimes. No one would be punished. A Muslim would be victimised, a Bosniak, a Croat, and the perpetrators could be assured of no punishment. There was Dr. Stakic who was supposed to, according to his mandate, provide for the security of the citizens. He did not do that, for those who were Bosniak and Croat. Your Honour, we heard live in this case one rape victim, only one, and the Defence made the point that Dr. Stakic probably didn't know -- wouldn't have known about the rape and asked repeated questions of the victim. And I'm certainly not criticising the Defence, but -- whether she had reported it to the authorities in Prijedor, and she said no, she did not. And on redirect we asked her why. And she answered - and this was a woman who had lost almost all of her family, had been killed, brutally killed in her village and in surrounding villages - she said, "To whom would I report it to? What sort of authorities were there, I'd like to know? Should I go and tell them and have my head cut off?" Why is Dr. Stakic responsible? Why does he bear criminal responsibility for that rape and all of the others? Because this is the atmosphere that was created, this atmosphere of complete impunity, that Muslims and Croats could be victimised because they were the proponents of the jihad, they had the plan. In one of his interviews, Dr. Stakic says that they found lists that every Serb -- every non-Serb had a list of the neighbour, the Serb they were supposed to kill. This kind of propaganda and paranoia reigned rather than any order or any attempt to dissuade any crime against non-Serbs. The accused had the power to name prosecutes and judges. He had access to the press. What would have happened if Dr. Stakic had in those interviews said, "Well, the Omarska camp, the police are -- have detained innocent individuals like Esad Sadikovic, like women who are doctors, professionals, judges, who have nothing to do and are no threat"? Would that camp have remained open? Would the citizens of Prijedor have allowed it? I don't believe so. Why is it that these crimes happened in Prijedor so much more than in any other part of the country, particularly of the Krajina? If you look at a document - I believe it's S281-3, which is the -- from Ms. Tabeau's report - she lists killings in the Bosnian Krajina in 19 different municipalities. 60 per cent of those killings took place in Prijedor, although Prijedor was a smaller municipality than Banja Luka, for example. There were about a half a million people in the Krajina, so Prijedor had only a little over 20 per cent of the entire population but over 60 per cent of the killings happened in Prijedor. Why couldn't Dr. Stakic have removed Simo Drljaca, told the Interior Minister to get rid of him, Simo Drljaca who signed the death warrant for these 125 men on the 5th of August? He didn't get rid of him because he was his ally, because they were engaged together in the same criminal enterprise. Dr. Stakic not only didn't try to get rid of Simo Drljaca, but when he came back as president, Simo Drljaca was brought back with him to serve again as chief of police. Simo Drljaca who had ran for Dr. Stakic the Omarska camp. And when Simo Drljaca in 1997 was killed resisting arrest, despite the time that by then so many of these crimes had been discovered, were widely known, Dr. Stakic spoke at his commemoration - this was corroborated by Ranko Travar, who also is mentioned in S375, the very short article, as being present and said he was there and Dr. Stakic was there and Dr. Stakic spoke - and what did Dr. Stakic say about the mass murder of Simo Drljaca? He said, "Although Simo Drljaca was killed, his great work will live on for the benefit of future generations." This would be an appropriate time for a break. I don't have a whole lot more, Your Honour. I think about a half hour more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned only till ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And let us now hear the final closing arguments by the Prosecution. Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If S64 could be put on the computer screen. Your Honour, the civilian authorities and Dr. Stakic exercised authority to arrest, to hold, and detain people regularly when they were Muslims and Croats. This document, S64, also shows that the authorities -- this is a document signed S. Milomir in the familiar signature with a seal on it. It's directed to Simo Drljaca. It indicates "All Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake are hereby released from further imprisonment." And I think later in that document it indicates that Simo Drljaca is delegated with authority to decide who would be released. So instead of Dr. Stakic exercising authority, encouraging using his influence, encouraging that perpetrator, that killers be brought to justice, he hands to the infamous Simo Drljaca the authority to release Serbs imprisoned by mistake. Clearly an intent, again, to allow impunity for those who are committing crimes against non-Serbs, against Muslims, and against Croats. The Crisis Staff, the SDS authorities, and Dr. Stakic could see to it that a person as high as Mohammed Cehajic, the elected president, was arrested, the president of the multi-ethnic assembly. Surely they could have seen to the arrest, the detention, the minimum for -- a minimum the dismissal of the police and army members who were perpetrating tortures and killings, such as Zoran Babic and Dado Mrdja from the intervention squad and so many others, including Simo Drljaca himself. Your Honour, what was going on in Prijedor in those few months before the journalist visit was on such a scale that even Dr. Stakic in one brief reference refers to it and calls it -- refers to the word "genocide." And I'd like to -- it's part of his S187 interview. It's when he's talking about why they're arranging for transport, so the Muslims will leave Prijedor. And if we could listen to this portion of the transcript of S187, again, a small portion, but something we might have missed in this 45-minute interview, but focus on the end of this segment when he talks about what in Europe is called "genocide."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When we came here, we drove past the town of Kozarac. I understand there was a big battle there. What happened in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] That is precisely where that Muslim extremism escalated because Kozarac, with its surroundings, had around 20.000 Muslims. And in Kozarac itself, which has 10 to 12 thousand, we found original lists with three and a half thousand, or to be precise, 3.791 members of the legal Muslim Territorial Defence, the number of each gun, and the date on which they were issued, and other light and medium heavy weapons. We had indications that this existed before. However, the fact and the moment when they came out to the Prijedor-Banja Luka main road and blocked around 10 kilometres of it at the entrance to and exit from that territory and all local access roads, the army -- actually, we made a decision that the army and the police go up there and lift the blockade of that road and that they withdraw at least 100 metres from the road into the depth of the territory that, nobody would enter deeper into their territory there. But that road not only links these two towns but even broader, these regions, and at the approach of the first police and military vehicle they opened fire without warning. After that, clashes followed and all that happened subsequently. You also saw a large number of destroyed houses and so on. Slowly life is returning to normal up there too. We have some people who were up there who barely managed to survive, who took refuge and who have now returned. We have a small number of people, refugees from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina who fled, and so we offer them accommodation. There are some Croats, there are some Ukraines and Ruthenians who do not mind anything, either these new authorities or the politics, and who stayed up there to live in their houses. A lot of them have also had their family homes destroyed. And I, as the mayor, and with my executive authorities, we are trying to compensate them for this, either with another house or an apartment, to secure a roof over their heads. We have managed to repair both the electric power network and the waterworks to an extent so that they may have electricity, along with the same power cuts, of course, as the other citizens of Prijedor municipality. And where are the Muslims who used to live in Kozarac? Well, Trnopolje was mainly filled with Muslims from Kozarac. A good part of those extremists were from Kozarac and they went to Trnopolje. The 1.500 and some men who were moved with the help of the International Red Cross to Karlovac were mostly from Kozarac. Then comes the reuniting of families in keeping with the Geneva Convention. And their families follow them and join them and so on. The rest, because their family homes had been destroyed, were accommodated either in the territory of Prijedor municipality or went, were transferred to -- some did go to Central Bosnia, those who expressed this wish. We organised buses and a train for them, and this was for free, just so that they go, so that there should be no casualties, that the genocide that we have already been blamed for in Europe should not occur. It is better that they leave, and tomorrow, when the war ends, and depending on the agreement of the level of the newly-formed states, which I am convinced will be created in this territory, those among them who want to return here will be able to do so."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the genocide that Dr. Stakic is referring to are all those actions that took place before the eyes of the world began to focus on Prijedor. There's a couple of other interesting - if I could regress a moment - a couple other interesting portions of the tape that we just played that again show the close cooperation of Dr. Stakic with the army and police. In talking about the attack on Kozarac, he says, beginning at the very top of 8485, the page ending in that ERN, "The army --" and then he stops and says, "actually, we made a decision that the army and the police go up there and lift the blockade." It's also interesting that he refers to himself again as the mayor. And he said, "I as the mayor, with my executive authorities," and he talks about using those authorities to compensate individuals, apparently Ukrainians and Ruthenians and refugees from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, presumably Serbs, and to take care of them. At the same time that the only thing he's doing for the Muslims and making sure that they leave. As he says, "It is better that they leave." He goes on to say, "And tomorrow when the war ends, depending on the agreement, they might be allowed to return." But clearly his policy was to cleanse that territory of Prijedor. Your Honour, in these few months, Your Honours, what we have observed is what we call genocide. We saw that tens of thousands of peoples lost their homes. They were destroyed not in fighting but they were destroyed by arson, by intentional destruction. Many thousands of people were detained under horrific conditions in camps. You know, bodies are very difficult to count -- to mean anything when you get into numbers as high as we're talking about. We know that over 100 died in the room 3 massacre, 125 on that August 5th convoy, buses that left the Omarska camp, that came originally from Keraterm, 220 or so in Vlasic Mountain, and a total of over 2.000, maybe 3.000 people dying during the indictment period, dying basically until the journalists came and the world attention focussed on Prijedor. The numbers don't mean much to us. Obviously to those people in that book of missing and their relatives it means a lot. The people who testified, so many of them, lost -- Mirza Mujadzic lost his grandfather and uncles. (redacted) carried his father's headless body from the Ljubija stadium. Ivo Atlija talked about hiding in the bushes while his father was killed a short distance away and later burying his body, the body of his father and so many members of this little village that he came from, Brisevo, so many of his neighbours and family members, including women, children, and invalids. Because of the nature of Bosnian society, we don't know how many women were raped but we know that rapes were happening in these camps and outside of the camps, and we know that tens of thousands of people were forced to leave Prijedor under the terror that was reigning. They were forced to believe that everything that was possible was done to make sure that community was destroyed and would not to return. Not only were their houses destroyed, their property was confiscated. There did become a point where I think the authorities realised they were better off confiscating a house and giving it to a Serb refugee than destroying it, and they began to do that. But they confiscated all of the vehicles and personal property. They destroyed the places of worship, virtually all of them in Prijedor, the churches and mosques. And in a particular -- particularly cruel method, so many people were taken away without any indication of where they went. Their loved ones do not know what happened to them. Their graves are not discovered. Their bodies are not known. So people like Witness X testified the last touch from his father was when his father pushed him on the back over the hill at Vlasic Mountain, saved his life, and he's never seen his father again. He doesn't know for sure. He presumes his father died in that massacre. Samir Poljak never saw his father after he was taken out of the Omarska camp. And Minka -- Dr. Minka Cehajic never knew what happened to her husband for sure after he was taken to the Omarska camp. Thousands of people in Prijedor are like that. They don't have a grave to visit for their loved ones. They don't even have the complete certainty of knowing where their bones lie or even the complete certainty of knowing that they are dead, although all reason tells them that. It's interesting, Your Honours, that the Defence case started in November and they presented approximately 45 witnesses. The Defence attorneys, I'd like to say, fought very hard in this case, and I did not always agree with them but I respect the professional job and the -- and the very active advocacy that they did and professional advocacy on behalf of their client. They presented a lot of witnesses, but throughout all of those months of the Defence case we have not heard of one single Muslim or Croat that Dr. Stakic, the president of the municipality, helped in Prijedor during this reign of terror, not one single instance when he used his power to do anything for an individual, to do anything to stop the crimes that were happening. We've seen many interviews with the accused on the television and the newspapers talking about the events, but we haven't heard him utter one word of regret for the crimes that happened under his leadership, for the thousands of people in Prijedor, the citizens of his municipality, who were killed, not one regret. All we heard were excuses, shifting the blame to the victims. And throughout the 11 years since these crimes happened we haven't heard -- we've talked to many people, many Defence witnesses, who knew Dr. Stakic, relatives, friends. We only heard evidence one time that I recall, and it was a 92 bis declaration, of Dr. Stakic indicating emotion and regret. And that was the 92 bis statements regarding his in-laws who wanted to avoid military service. And according to the statement, Dr. Stakic -- the statements, Dr. Stakic's eyes filled with tears from the fact that, in one case it was someone in 1991, and the other case was, I believe, an individual outside of Prijedor -- that Dr. Stakic could not do anything to help these in-laws avoid military service. His eyes filled with tears about that. But for the thousands of people in Prijedor who died, who lost their homes, who were raped, tortured, we haven't heard one word of empathy from the accused in the 11 years that have passed since this crime happened, even in the months of the case of the Defence that has been presented and all of his friends and associates who testified. The logical conclusion is Dr. Stakic does not regret the crimes. He planned the crimes. He coordinated with those perpetrating the crimes. They were his intent. There's one man, the man who Dr. Stakic replaced, Professor Mohammed Cehajic, that we asked many witnesses about, and Dr. Stakic never expressed -- never talked about him, never expressed a word of regret or a question of what happened to him. Professor Cehajic, all the witnesses say, was an admired man. I recall the secretary, who obviously wanted very much to testify in favour of Dr. Stakic but also said that Professor Cehajic was very polite, very proper. All of the witnesses have said that he was polite, generous. We even have an interview with Dr. Stakic where he talks about the planning for the takeover. It's S47. And he mentions in that article - it's a 1994 Kozarski Vjesnik article - he mentions Professor Cehajic congratulating him after he is made the president of the new Serb assembly in January. And Professor Cehajic says, "I congratulate you with all my heart. Now we're both presidents." And Dr. Stakic said in the interview, "But I knew what was behind the smile, the plan, the terrible plan that the Muslims had for us." And yet Kozarski Vjesnik and many of the other evidence we have and witnesses say that the only thing that Professor Cehajic advocated after the forcible takeover and overthrow of the elected government that he headed was a Ghandian resistance. Even in one of the Kozarski Vjesnik articles he's identified in 1994 as one of the leaders of the Ghandian resistance. Professor Cehajic was a simple professor of a high school. He liked to spend time with his son and his wife. There's never any -- there's not one bit of evidence that he advocated any violence, and he was the person who was elected. And unlike myself, he was a person chosen by the people of Prijedor to speak on their behalf, and he suffered like so many of them did. So I think it's appropriate to hear a little bit of his words. This is a portion, a small portion, of the letter he wrote to his wife, delivered from an inmate from the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "Since my departure, since that 23rd of May when they came to my house to get me, I have been living in another world. It seems to me that everything that is happening to me is just an ugly dream, just a nightmare. And I simply cannot understand how something like this is possible. My dear Minka, Almira, and my son, you know how much I love you, you know how much I love you all. And because of this love, I have never done anything nor would I ever do anything that would cause you any pain. I know that you know that what they're trying to put on me has nothing to do with me whatsoever. I just keep wondering whom and how much I have offended so that I have to go through all this. But I still believe in justice and I believe in truth, and I believe that this will all be cleared up."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence in this case shows that the accused played a key role in crimes of just tremendous magnitude, the deaths of thousands, the deportations of tens of thousands. Your Honours, this Tribunal was created to bring justice for these kinds of crimes, and crimes of this magnitude, a person who played the key role -- a key role in those crimes, such as Dr. Stakic, it is our position that the justice requires a sentence of life in prison for these crimes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes today's hearing. And we will hear the closing arguments Monday morning, 9.30, presented by the Defence, starting in Courtroom II and then later in Courtroom I in the afternoon. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
